Mr. W. F. KAY (Brome-Missisquoi) presented the fourth report of the select standing committee on Agriculture and Colonization as follows:
Your committee has had under consideration the order of reference respecting the- cattle industry, with power to examine into the whole situation, and to recommend such measures as would, in the opinion of this committee, be beneficial to the further development of that industry, and after consideration of this matter, recommend to the House the following resolutions as passed separately by this committee at a meeting held this day, namely:
(1)	That this committee recommend that a Canadian representative at Washington should be appointed at once.
(2)	That this committee recommend that the government enter into negotiations with the United States looking toward the entry of Canadian cattle into the United States market on more favourable terms than at present.
(3)	That this committee recommend that the Canadian customs tariff against the United States cattle should be placed on the same rate and same specific basis as the United States tariff against Canadian cattle, with a provision that if the United States tariff duties be removed ot reduced, the Canadian duties would thereupon be removed or reduced to the same extent.

Mr. PAUL MERCIER (St. Henri) presented the third and final report of the special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise as follows:
The Special Committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise, beg leave to present the following as their Third and Final Report:
1.	On the 5th February 1926 the House of Commons adopted the following resolution:
That a Special Committee of this House, consisting of nine members, be appointed forthwith to

Customs Inquiry-Report
investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise and alleged serious losses to the public treasury because of inefficiency or corruption on the part of officers of the Department and others, and that such investigation extend back over such period of time as the Committee may decide and have regard to all matters affecting the prevention of smuggling, the prosecution of offenders, the seizure, storage and disposal of smuggled goods, or goods seized for purposes of excise or other taxes, the appraisal of goods for revenue purposes, the collection of customs and excise duties, the knowledge of ministers or officials of offences or irregularities affecting the public service in said department, the efficiency of the administration thereof, and the necessity of safeguarding the public revenue and the public treasury, and that such Committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, to adjourn from place to place, to print the evidence taken before the Committee, and to report from time to time.
2.	By a subsequent resolution the Committee was constituted as follows:
Messrs. C. W. Bell, K.C. (Hamilton West), Hon. R. B. Bennett, K.C., D. Donaghy, K.C., A. J. Doucet, J. C. Elliott, K.C., D. M. Kennedy, P. Mercier, K.C. (St. Henri), E. C. St. Pere, Hon. H. H. Stevens.
Mr. Paul Mercier, K.C. was elected Chairman. Mr. Elliott having been appointed a Minister of the Crown and by resolution of the House of Commons Mr. William T. Goodison was appointed to the vacancy so created, on March 15th 1926.'
3.	Your Committee sat from 9th February to 11th June, held 115 sittings, and heard 224 witnesses. Mr. R. L. Calder, K.C. was appointed Counsel to the Committee and Mr. R. D. Tighe, Assistant Counsel, both appointments being ratified by the House. Certain interested parties were represented by Counsel on a number of the hearings, by leave of the Committee.
4.	Notwithstanding the time devoted by the Committee to the taking of evidence the matters referred to it by the order of reference could not be completely reviewed. Much evidence was taken in connection with the Port of Montreal: the situation at Beebe and Rock Island, Quebec: and the operation of distilleries. The commiittee have also with some detail examined into iliquor smuggling in the Maritime Provinces. The committee have examined in a general way the conduct of business at certain customs ports of Ontario. The committee have not dealt, except incidentialiy, with the Middle West and the Pacific Coast. To a degree, therefore, this report is incomplete and suggestive rather than final. Full audit and extradepartmental investigation would be profitable in improving the service and recovering a large amount of revenue.
5.	Since 1897 the Customs Department has been under the control of s responsible Minister. In 1918 the Department of Excise, which had been a separate department of the Public Service since the year 1868 was amalgamated with the Customs Department and in 1920 and 1924 respectively the amalgamated departments were charged with the collection of sales and Income Taxes. The administration of these amalgamated departments is a serious task. The Customs frontier between the United States and Canada is a very long one and the position and number of bridges and highways crossing the boundary together with the extended line of sea coast rendered the suppression of smuggling difficult. The adoption by the United States of the Eighteenth Amendment has increased the difficulty, because it has made the incentive to illegally convey intoxicating liquor to the United States very great, and with the mass production of many products in that country there is a correspondingly great
incentive to illegally import such products into Canada. In the year 1925 smuggling assumed such large proportions that a number of business men made representations .to the Government, in consequence of which an Act, Chapter 39 of the Statutes of 1925, was passed making smuggling an indictable offence, where the goods were of the value of more than $200 and the penalties incurred by such smuggling increased.
6.	The evidence submitted to the Committee leads to the general conclusion that for a long time the Department of Customs and Excise had been slowly degenerating in efficiency and that the process was greatly accelerated in the last few years. Apparently the Hon. Jacques Bureau, then Minister of Customs, failed to appreciate and properly discharge the responsibilities of his office and as a result there was a lack of efficient, continuous and vigorous control of subordinates by the Headquarters Staff at Ottawa.
7.	The procedure provided by the Customs Act in the matter of Customs seizures is as follows: Upon making a seizure the Collector or Seizing Officer forthwith reports the circumstances of the case to the Commissioner of Customs (Section 174). Thereupon the Commissioner notifies the owner or claimant of the thing seized, stating the reasons for the seizure, and calls upon such owner or claimant to furnish within thirty days any evidence he may desire to submit. (Section 175). After the expiration of thirty days or sooner, if evidence is forthcoming on the part of the owner or claimant, "the Commissioner may consider and weigh the circumstances of the case and report his opinion and recommendation thereon to the Minister." (Section 176). The Minister thereupon either gives his decision and states the terms upon which the thing seized or detained may be released or the penalty or forfeiture remitted or refers the decision to the Court (Section 177). The Committee finds that this procedure was not followed. Although, as a rule, the facts are correctly recited in the summary submitted to the Minister, the opinion is not infrequently at variance with such facts, and the recommendation is so drawn as to elicit a decision to which such facts are repugnant. This discrepancy is accounted for by the fact that the report upon the evidence was in many instances preceded by a conference, and the recommendation was dictated by an intelligent anticipation of the Minister's wishes in the premises.
8.	The Committee is of opinion that the administrative duties of the Department of Customs and Excise should be left to the Executive Officers of the Department. Where the value of the goods or the amount in question is $200 or more the procedure should be automatic and not subject to Ministerial interference or control. Where the goods in question are under $200 the case would fall under the heading of "Petty Offences" and the Minister's discretion might there find a proper field for its exercise.
9.	The Committee finds that theft of motor vehicles
has frequently been associated with smuggling on the Quebec Customs frontier. The procedure followed by the Department in dealing with cars stolen and smuggled has resulted	in	an advantage to	the	thief
and receiver as against the owner of the car.
In the opinion of the Committee the procedure might be modified so as to provide that when the owner has established his title to the satisfaction of the department the car should	be	forthwith released to	him,under bonds to re-export it, and upon payment of charges for storage, etc., such release to be made at a time and place of which notice should be given to the person in whose possession it was at time of seizure in order that	he	may take such	legal	proceedings as are competent	to him to assert	any	claim
thereto or lien thereupon.
10.	The Committee find that it is the common practice of the Department to grant clearances to vessels

wholly or partly laden with liquor for the United States, or allegedly bound for a foreign port, but admittedly sailing to "rum rows," and that false landing certificates have been produced to obtain cancellation of bonds given for foreign export of cargoes so cleared.
The Committee further finds that a strong presumption is raised that some proportion of the liquor so shipped and cleared finds its way back into Canada for consumption. The Committee, therefore, recommend that excise and sales tax be levied on all Canadian made intoxicating liquors released from bond, no matter where they are carried and consumed, and that duty and sales tax be levied on all alcoholic liquors entering Canada, whether in bond or otherwise, irrespective of their ultimate destination.
Doubts have been cast upon the sufficiency of existing legislation to prohibit or authorize regulations prohibiting the illegal export of intoxicating liquors to the United States. To the extent to which such legislation may be insufficient the Committee recommends that it be amended. The Committee further recommends that, as soon as possible, regulations be made to prohibit clearances being granted to vessels carrying liquor as cargo, sailing from a Canadian Port to a United States Port, such regulations to make an exception in favour of liquor being imported into the United States in accordance with the laws of that Country.
11.	Subsection 4 of Section 171 of the "Excise Act" provides that "no spirits subject to excise which have not been warehoused for at least two years shall be entered for consumption". By reason of special circumstances arising out of the War, Parliament on the 1st day of July, 1920, Chapter 52, 10-11 George Fifth, Section 4, amended the section by adding thereto a . proviso empowering the Governor General to suspend the operations of the said subsection during such period or periods as he may deem necessary. From sessional paper No. 84, 1926, it appears that by Order in Council the following distilleries have been permitted to enter for consumption the spirits manufactured during the period of nine months or less from the date of distillation:
Gooderham & Worts, P.C. 641, April 17t.h, 1924.
Distillery Corporation Limited, P.C. 1646, September 14th, 1925.
Manitoba Refinery Company (Ltd), P.C. 1903, October 20th, 1925.
Consolidated Distilleries of Manitoba, P.C. 29, January 7th, 1926.
In the oipinion of the committee such unmatured spirits are unfit for human consumption and their release is injurious to the public health. The committee therefore recommends that Section 4 of Chapter 52, 10-11 George Fifth, be repealed at the present session of parliament and that the orders in council issued thereunder be, thereupon forthwith, cancelled. The committee further recommends that the technical regulations now governing the denaturing of alcohol be revised by competent experts so as to render all classes of denatured alcohol non-potable, and that where the Regulations under Section 171 of the Excise Act provide for the warehousing of potable liquors they shall provide for the maturing of such liquor in wood for a period of at least two years.
' 12.* The committee recommends that the following firms and companies should be proceeded against in the proper forum to recover the sums, if any, now owing by them to the Crown:
John Gaunt Company.

B. B. Glove Co.

Telford & Chapman.

O.	B. Earle Co.

With reference to the distilleries, the committee has not had time to investigate them all. The committee recommends that a thorough audit and examination be made of the records and accounts of all the distilleries in respect of all matters relating to a loss of customs, excise and sales tax revenue.
13.	The committee finds that the following officers have been delinquent in their duties and recommends that their sendees be dispensed with:
1.	R. P. Clerk, Inspector of the port of Montreal.
2.	A. E. Giroux, Superintendent of Customs and Excise, Montreal.
3.	W Duval, Preventive Officer at Montreal.
4.	John Landv, Customs Officer, Montreal.
5.	Collector E. Brownlee, of Beebe, Quebec.
6.	Marvin A. Sawyer, Customs Officer at Rock Island, and that in the interest of the public service arrangements should be made for the retirement of the following persons:
1.	R. R. Farrow, Deputy Minister.
2.	W. S. Weldon, Collector of Customs at Montreal.
3.	Henry McLaughlin, Surveyor of Customs at the port of Montreal.
14.	The committee recommends that the conduct of the officers at the port of Windsor, Ontario, and other important ports, should be further investigated and that the services of such of them as are found guilty of evasion of duty should be dispensed with.
15.	The committee recommends that the evidence of J. A. E. Bisaillon given before this committee with reference to his bank account for the amount of S69.000 be transmitted to the Attorney-General for Quebec, for the purpose of comparison with the evidence given by him on the same point at preliminary inquiry at Quebec, P.Q., in the case of Rex vs Symons et al, and for such action by the said Attorney-General as the evidence may warrant; and further that the evidence in connection with the Morris Delage Motor Car case be transmitted to the said Attorney-General for such further action as the said evidence may warrant.
16.	The committee recommends that for reasons of sound economy and increased efficiency there should be a reduction made in the number of ports of entry into Canada.
In support of this recommendation the committee would call attention to the following facts:
The United States has 270 customs ports of entry. The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland has 80 ports of entry. On the other hand, Canada has a total of 681 places at which customs revenue is collected.

Customs Inquiry-Report
17.	For the prevention of smuggling and of other frauds a strong preventive force under a capable administrator is necessary, and the committee, therefore, recommends:
1.	That the Preventive Service be re-organized under a Chief, possessed with the highest qualifications for such office, clothed with wide powers of initiative, direction and control.
2.	That such Chief Preventive Officer be authorized to select his staff in consultation with the Civil Service Commission.
3.	That the Chief Preventive Officer be authorized to organize within the Preventive Service a secret service force, with special training in criminal investigation work, which force shall be under the general executive direction of the Chief of the Preventive Service.
4.	That Preventive Officers and persons authorized to act as Customs and Excise Officers be given power to arrest without a warrant persons found committing any act declared by the Customs and Excise Acts to be an indictable offence.
5.	That in connection with Preventive Service work the R.C.M.P. services be used for Patrol Work on the border, and while so engaged they be given full powers as Customs Officers. Pending the reorganization of the Preventive Service the R.C.M.P. should be immediately detailed for Patrol Service on all important points on the Border.
18.	The evidence adduced before the Committee disclosed two outstanding facts, namely-
First, the methods of appraisal are exceedingly careless and fail to safeguard the interests of the importer or the revenues of the Country from being defrauded by undervaluation, and
Secondly, persons appointed as appraisers are in many instances untrained in the branch to which they are appointed.
The Committee recommend that the appraisal branch be re-organized and that all appraisers be chosen because of their competency to estimate the values of the class of goods they are appointed to appraise.
19.	The Committee recommends that in future 'the provisions of Sections 213 and 213a of the Customs Act, which provide for the removal of buildings within a hundred yards of the boundary which are made use of in smuggling operations, be strictly enforced.
The situation created by the location of Derby Line, Vermont, and Rock Island, Quebec, as brought to the attention of the Committee is of a grave nature, and they recommend that a bond be established in each factory in which bond goods imported from the United States shall be placed until released for manufacturing purposes, and that an officer be appointed to look after such bond at the owner's expense.
20.	The Committee recommends that Schedule "C" Prohibited Goods, of the Customs Act, be amended to include merchandise which is marked in contravention of the Gold and Silver Marking Act. That Act provides for prohibition of the importation of articles improperly marked, but Customs Officers ordinarily are not acquainted with the provisions of the Act, and for this reason the Committee recommends the inclusion of the prohibition in schedule "C" of the Customs Act.
21.	Where articles containing precious metals are seized and forfeited the Committee recommends that they be not sold in the open market, as at present, but should be melted down and disposed of as bullion.
22.	The Committee recommends that the regulations governing the distribution of the proceeds of fines and forfeitures be revised and that more liberal treatment be accorded informers and seizing officers. The moieties granted seizing officers in respect of seizures made
14011-298*
by them should not however, be distributed to such officers as each seizure is made. Such moieties should be paid into a special fund and periodically distributed to all the members of the Customs and Preventive Services.
23.	The Committee recommends that in cases of commercial smuggling or under-valuation, where the offenders are known, they should at once be arrested and brought to trial with the utmost promptness. The Committee further recommends that the Department of Justice be requested to select at once capable and experienced Counsel in important centres, and retain them to act for the Department of Customs and Excise in all future cases.
24.	The real solution of the difficulties at such points as Windsor, Niagara Falls, where traffic is heavy, and where a thorough examination of vessels and vehicles cannot be carried out, will be found in the discovery in advance by investigators of the secret sendee of the persons who make a practice of smuggling at these points, and their arrest when passing the Customs barrier. The Committee recommends that at bridges, ferries and main highways, where traffic enters Canada, in addition to the regular Customs supervision, vessels and vehicles should 'be searched at frequent, irregular and uncertain times. The uncertainty as to what vehicles will be examined, and as to when such examinations will be made, should operate as a strong deterrent of smuggling.
Your Committee recommend that such of the account books and other books and papers belonging to the firms mentioned in Clause Twelve of this Report, as may be necessary for use in any action that may be taken against the said firms, be retained by the House in order that they may be available if required.
Your Committee submit herewith for the information of the House, their Minutes of Proceedings and the Evidence taken by them.

subtopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE BY MR. KENNEDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. During the debate on the petition of J. A. Collins I considered that the ordinary proprieties demanded that I should absent myself from the chamber. To-day when reading Hansard I found the following statement by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) which appears in the second column of page 4630 of Hansard -for June 16, 1926:
I have heard rumours that the hon. gentleman will get the Chiltern Hundreds; that after he has served

his day and generation through this section and done his full share to keep this government in office, he will get some nominal job in order that the seat may be vacated.
In view of that statement, and in view of the fact that I have been impressed by some of the arguments made in both debates, I think I ought to explain my position with regard to this contentious affair.
I deny absolutely the truth of any such rumour on which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) may have based his statement. I have not been promised directly or indirectly anything, and I would consider it an insult to have any such proposition made to me. I would not accept anything if it were offered to me.
The petition under the Controverted Elections Act was duly filled by one Page, in the Supreme Court of Alberta. The charges in that petition are both serious and comprehensive, so serious that they appear to embrace every -crime which it would be possible to commit under our election laws, so comprehensive that they include every method by which those crimes could be perpetrated. I naturally felt that I owed it to myself, to my constituents, and to this House of which I a:m a member, to disprove those charges, that is, the ptersoniali charges, and that is all I am interested -in so far as the petition is concerned, -and I considered that the proper place to do so was upon the trial of that petition.
A rumour was circulated some time ago that the petitioner wais likely to withdraw his petition, but this could not be done without leav-e of the court, and even if the petitioner remained inactive, another person could be substituted for him. Immediately the rumour reached me, I instructed my solicitors that it was my intention to press the petition myself to trial, which attitude I had already indicated in my previous statement to this House.
It has beten stated that iby virtue of the provisions of section 91 of the Dominion Elections Act, no evidence could be given upon the hearing of the petition by voters as to whom they voted for. It is conceded that such is an accurate Statement of the law. Such evidence was receivable and given in the criminal prosecution of Robb, when 110 parties testified that they voted at one poll for Collins, who actually received, only 21 votes at that poll, so that if the -evidence of each of them were true, Mr. Colins was deprived of 89 votes at that pol. It should, however, -be borne in mind that the jury's verdict of guilty does not necessarily mean such to -be th-e -case. Robb was not accused of switching 89 votes, but merely of switching

Peace River Election
votes, no number naturally being mentioned, and1 if the jury had believed only one of these 110 witnesses, it would have been sufficient to justify their verdict.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. In my opinion the hon. member has gone far beyond his righit already, but inasmuch as he conceives it to be his privilege * to conduct a debate all alone by himsellf, when nobody has an opportunity to reply, I think it is my duty to intervene. Undoubtedly he has exceeded his privilege, and he reached the end of it when he denied the rumour which I stated here.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE BY MR. KENNEDY
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, when an hon. member rises in the House to give his personal explanation, he must confine himself to the question of privilege, and not go beyond the limits which are permissible under the rules. I would ask the hon. gentleman to state briefly what he has to say in denial but not to reopen this whole debate.
Right Hon. W. L..MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, I think I
ought to direct your attention to the circumstance that the hon. member who is now speaking absented himself from the House during the course of the debate which took place, and had no opportunity whatever of denying the statement made concerning himself at that time. I think my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) took full latitude when he was debating the motion before the House the other day, and I think he should now be prepared to allow the fullest latitude to the hon. member to state his position.
Mr. M-EIGHEN:	The hon.1 member
absented himself, it is true, and rightly so, but his absenting himself from the debate was because of the same reason which even if there were no other, would prevent him speaking now. If he could absent himself from the debate when the matter ought to be discussed in order to debate it alone when it cannot be discussed, then, of course, the logic of the Prime Minister is right. I do not object at all to his denying anything which was said against him if he believes that anything said against him was untrue as a matter of fact, but beyond that he has absolutely no right to go. What is more it is so manifest he has no right that he knows it himself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE BY MR. KENNEDY
speechtext:
I have been thirty years in parliament, and I will take my own experience on matters of privilege in connection with similar cases to the one which
now occupies the attention of the House.
If the seat attributed to a member is put in question the member has to withdraw, under the rules of the House, when the matter is being discussed. That is the law of parliament. I was in a similar situation myself, five years ago, because the petitioner not having proceeded with his petition I had failed to resign within the legal delays from one seat after having been elected for two. When the question came before the House, under the rules I had to withdraw after I had made my statement.
In this case, the debate arose the day before yesterday on the petition of Collins. The hon. gentleman withdrew, as it was his duty to do; he also withdrew a few weeks ago when the first petition was under discussion. I now gather from the remarks made by the hon. gentleman that he complains of a certain statement made during his absence from the House by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), namely, that there was a rumour to the effect that the hon. gentleman would take the Chiltern Hundreds. We all know what that means under the British parliamentary system. It is a fiction of the law by which a member wishing to resign accepts an insignificant position under the crown to disqualify him from sitting any longer as a member of the House of Commons, The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) complains of that statement, and rightly so if it is not true, and his privilege to rise today to contradict that statement must be confined to that point. If he has any other matter to complain of affecting his honour, let him make that other point, but he cannot reopen the debate. He would be going beyond his privilege by reopening the debate. I have not the paragraph under my hand in Bourinot, but it is well known that no member can reopen a past debate by referring to Hansard and giving explanations about matters that came up when he was not in the House. Briefly the hon. gentleman is perfectly right in rising to a question of privilege, and denying any rumour or accusation affecting his honour, but beyond that he is not in order.

speechtext: I am large enough in person, I think, to be seen, but twice during the present week, on leaving this House, I have with difficulty escaped collision with motor cars which, after passing the police at the gates, have assumed a speed that would not be allowed in any city such as Montreal, and I think some rule or regulation should be made limiting that speed, so that members leaving after the House closes may be free from accidents of that character.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: DANGEROUS SPEEDING ON PARLIAMENT HILL AND 'WELLINGTON STREET

Will the minister explain why there is such a large increase in this vote this year? I am rather astonished to learn the country is paying annually a million and a half dollars for the administration of the Grain Act, which has to do very largely with the marketing of Canada's premier crop-a crop that last year ran to nearly $500,000,000. I know of no other line of business where the government pays such high administration expenses without loading any portion of it upon the trade itself. Take the insurance business; when the salary of the superintendent of insurance was increased from $5,000 to $10,000, one-half of the increase was loaded upon the insurance companies notwithstanding their protests. I do not see why the grain trade should not bear the expense of administering this act. Why should a taxpayer in the province of New Brunswick have to pay any portion of it? It does not seem to me to be fair or justifiable. At all events, the cost should be kept within limits, and if there is to be any increase in the service rendered I do not see why the cost should not be paid for by the trade itself. I am not making this statement merely for the purpose of hearing myself talk, I should like to know why the country is called upon to pay a million and .

a half dollars a year for the administration of this act when the expense could be imposed upon the trade itself, and ought to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a fair question, but my hon. friend is quite in error when he believes-sincerely I have no doubt -that there is a shortage. This particular business carries itself and shows a considerable surplus.

speechtext:
We got a little ahead a

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have never been charging interest or depreciation, but it is not a losing business. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And there was another reason. As we got along in the season the board asked for more money; climatic conditions having made it more expensive to handle the crop. previous year some $65,000. climatic conditions-to which I have just referred-and the establishment of additional inspections for points west and of appeal boards at Edmonton and Vancouver.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury has asked a very pertinent question relating to the elevators owned by xhe people of Canada. Take the Prince Rupert elevator, for instance. Hon. gentlemen will remember the debate we had on that. It was stated that the elevator could not be a success until such time as there was an outlet for the Peace River country and the grain could go through that elevator. We protested against the Halifax elevator, not because we did not want to see the grain go that way, but because we said the grain could not go by that route at the present railway rates, and we asked the government at that time to see that the rate was brought down so that our grain could go not only to Quebec, but to Halifax and St. John. Supply-Trade and Commerce

I deprecate more than I can say the introduction of regional discussions when a matter of this kind is before the committee. In the first place, the grain business is the backbone of prosperity in this country. The value of the crop raised in western Canada last year is reflected in the present appearance of prosperity in the east. That is clear. Do not have any doubt about it. My friends may not agree, but I can tell them that that is so.
The grain business in western Canada has been free from many of the difficulties that were encountered in connection with the development of the grain business of the United States. Why? Because we had a federal grain act; we had a law of universal application to all the provinces in the west, and in 1912-1913 we passed it, as the Canada Grain Act so that its application was universal throughout the Dominion and not only in that part of the Dominion which was west of the Great Lakes.
I recall not long ago being in England and being asked by a group of business men to explain to them the operations of the Canada Grain Act, and when they found that the farmer who carries his grain to the elevator, if he is dissatisfied witli the grade that is given by the purchaser of his grain, has the opportunity of having that grade determined through means that are provided by the government and paid for out of the revenues of this country, and subsequently recouped by the trade itself, they thought it was a wonderful system in so far as the grain trade is concerned. It is true that increased knowledge has taught us much with respect to it, and the establishment of a laboratory at Winnipeg to determine the moisture content of grain is of the utmost importance. In England, where they are purchasers mostly of supplies of grain from which they can produce their flour and bread, they have found it necessaiy to determine by the most scientific methods the moisture content of wheat, and matters of that kind. Now the reason, I would say to my friends from the east on this side of the House, for all this machinery with respect to the Grain Act is not because we desire to encourage expenditure by this country, for the grain itself pays the tolls that are necessary to enable these safeguards to be maintained. The object of all this machinery is to protect the producer of grain, to protect his product right from the time it leaves his farm. In every instance the sums that are paid are recouped by the tolls that are taken by the officials for the

service rendered, so that at the end of the year instead of it being a charge upon the public revenues it means that we have received a surplus. That is the position with respect to that feature.

I direct attention to that because it has seemed to me that at times there is not perhaps in the east a clear appreciation of the fact that the determination of the quality of grain and the moisture content, the supervision of the shipping, the weighing, and the general exercise by the grain commissioners of judicial functions-if I'may use that term because they are judicial functions-have enabled the

I regret to say that in my judgment in many instances, and I direct this to the attention of the minister, the men are not sufficiently well paid. When you go to Winnipeg or to Calgary during the grain movement and see the way in which millions of bushels of grain amounting in the aggregate to hundreds of millions of dollars in value are being sampled, you will realize the vast responsibility that is placed upon men who are too ill-paid for the services they render; and I am heartily in sympathy with any proposals that will increase the compensation paid to these men in the discharge of the responsibilities placed upon them. I hope that my hon. friends will not take serious umbrage at the observations I make as one who has in times past-perhaps unhappily no more- been interested in the grain business, and I have been interested in it very largely for many years. Now I have no longer any interest in it but at one time I had the interest of one who had money invested in the trade and was receiving very profitable returns therefrom. I have been greatly interested not only in the development of the business but also in the operations of the act. Now that I am no more interested in it I feel that I owe a duty, at least to those who produced the grain from which profits have been abundantly made in times past- I am very frank about it-to do everything I can to maintain the high efficiency of the elevator service under the act. I think that high efficiency will be, to some extent, bettered if the minister recognizes the responsibility of those who have duties to discharge under the Grain Act and sees that they are adequately and handsomely rewarded for the services they render.

speechtext: We might come back to the administration of the Canada Grain Act.

I desire to occupy a little of the time of the committee in discussing a matter which is of vital importance to my constituents and to the constituents of other hon. members in this House. There is great need
4 p.m. of a grain research laboratory, which, if it can bring about a change in tlhe standards governing the inspection of our grain, will render a great service to grain producers and the grain trade generally. The time is ripe for it; I think it is due.
We have heard during the last twenty years a great deal regarding the selling of wheat on a better basis than that of colour and weight; that is selling it on its strength and on its protein content, and I wish to say that a research laboratory can render very great service in that direction. Look at the manner in which our grain is graded at the present moment. I read to the House the definition of our grades of grain, as follows:
No. 1 Manitoba northern wheat shall include all varieties of hard red spring wheat equal in value to ''Marquis" wheat; shall be well matured and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 (pounds to the bushel and practically free of damaged kernels and foreign grains; shall contain 60 jper cenlt of hard red vitreous kernels.
Throughout that definition there is very little to indicate that strength forms a factor in grading our wheat. The number of pounds has nothing to do with it. The variety of wheat has something to do with it. Some varieties are stronger than others. The expression "red vitreous kernels" have been relied on to indicate the strength of the wheat. I wish to show that it is only in a general way that those words indicate the strength of the wheat. Before I come to that, it is recognized by all who are selling wheat, handling it, importing it or having anything to do with it, that Canadian wheat is very much desired in the markets of the world because of its strength and milling qualities. It is the wheat that is very strong in nitrogen and in protein that is desired by the millers of the world for the purpose of mixing with softer wheats and wheats that are lacking in those elements. Before dealing with that I wish to refer for a moment to another service that can be rendered by a research laboratory. There is a complaint for many years that bleached wheat which has been subject to a slight rain and discoloured only is not receiving its value at the present time according to our own inspection, and here is a service that the research laboratory can render. Referring to the evidence submitted by Dr. Birchard, who is now in charge of the research laboratory at Winnipeg, he makes two suggestions in regard to bleached wheat. He points out that his researches have shown clearly that this wheat has not been damaged for milling purposes. The same results have been obtained from researches carried on in other laboratories. It is found that the wheat has been slightly discoloured, that is all. Let us see what he says:
The first suggestion made was that wheat which has been slightly bleached on the outside should be regarded as sound and should not be considered as damaged wheat on account of bleaching only.

That is to say, slightly bleached wheat is to be 'considered sound1 provided it is not mouldy or sprouted or obviously inferior in some other respects. Experiments show that wheat which is only bleached on the outside and: in such a way as to reduce its grade from No. 1 northern to No. 3 northern does not lose its actual milling or baking value. It is true that sometimes there is a slight decrease in the test weight per bushel, but this authority points out that if that were serious it would be degraded on that account also. Further he says:
It is not contended that slightly bleached wheat weighing sixty-two pounds per bushel will give the same yield oif flour as wheat yielding sixty-four and a half pounds per bushel but it is contended that slightly bleached wheat will give the same amount of flour and of as good quality as that produced from No. 1 northern having the same test weight per bushel.	-
Summing up he says:
Slightly bleached wheat is as good in every respect as wheat of the same test weight per bushel and of the same kind and variety which has not been slightly bleached.
During all the years I have been growing and selling grain1-and1 I have been doing so for the last 'thirty years-grain that has been slightly bleached has been consistently degraded one or two grades, consequently falling in value seven and sometimes eight cents per bushel!. Yet here we find one chemist who tel'ls uis that such grain has not been damaged for miMing -purposes although it has slightly decreased in weight per bushel. I am discussing the question at this length to-day in order to show the difficulties that exist in the present system. In bulletin 37 of the laboratory of Minneapolis there appears on page six a paragraph dealing with the different percentages of protein in Various grades of wheat. I quote the following:
This illustrates the difficulty of classifying wheats on the basis of their texture-or the percentage of
dark, hard and vitreous kernel	as is
attempted in assigning samples of dark northern and dark spring sub-classes; the presumption is that the dark northern wheats will yield flour higher in percentage of crude protein than will the northern spring wheats. This has not proven to be the case in the samples examined of the last two crops. The average low volume follows the average protein content in both of these crops, when No. 1 dark northern and No. 1 northern spring wheat flour are contrasted; the advantage being in favour of the No. 1 northern flours in both seasons.	.
That i<s to say, those which were lightest in colour gave the beat results.
This suggests that careful consideration should be given to the possibility of classifying wheat on the basis of protein content rather than on the basis of the less tangible factor of the percentage of dark, hard

and vitreous kernels, since the true protein is determined with far greater precision and is probably more definitely related to baking strength than is the kernel texture.
At page 25 the same writer says:
No. 1 northern spring wheat flour contained a slightly higher percentage of protein than flour milled from No. 1 dark northern spring wheat.
In other words, the lighter wheat contained the stronger flour.
This suggests the inadequacy of the present system of classifying spring wheats on the basis of their density or the relative proportion of vitreous kernels present. A determination of the percentage of crude protein in the wheat would probably afford a more satisfactory and accurate basis of classification in the several sub-classes of northern spring wheat.

Manitoba wheat is not at present graded on a crude protein basis and as a result tihe grades overlap especially No. 2 and No. 3. This is what I wish to direct the attention of the committee to particularly:
The colour or quality of the grain is no indication of protein content.
I	hold in my hand a record of some tests that were made of western Canadian wheat in a private testing laboratory at Winnipeg. I am selecting the tests under letter C, not to give strength to my argument, but simply taking them as they come. These tests show protein content of 13.4; 13.7; 14.8; 11.8; 13.8; 13.2; 12; 12.2; and so on. Let me draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that in those tests of No. 1, appear samples that differ 3 per cent in protein content, the extremes being 14.8 and 11.8. What difference does that make in the price of the grain? Well, judging from the premiums that are paid on the American market it means a difference in price of at least 12 cents, or on the higher premium 25 cents a bushel. We have not such a system in Canada, but in the United States the common system is to pay a premium of from one to two and a half cents for each quarter of one per cent protein content. Yet according to our system these two samples of wheat are placed in the same grade, the farmer knows nothing about how strong or how weak his wheat is, and he receives the same price.
Let me point out that in the handling of all other products of the farm, cattle, hogs, eggs, and so on, the desire is to have them classified as nearly as possible according to their value, to have the choice steers, for example, put together, selecting as far as possible those of the same type and value, and naturally they bring better prices. Now, why should we be selling our grain in such a haphazard way that a man who is growing grain worth $1.60 a bushel gets the same price as the man who is growing grain worth only $1.50 a bushel? There is frequently that difference. This is a very distinct loss, as I will point out a little later, and it is no encouragement to farmers to grow the better types of grain.
What is protein? It is simply nitrogen that is stored up in the ground, finds its way into the leaves and stock of the wheat plant, and MOll-2991
at the proper time reaches the kernel, where with starch, sugar and mineral matter it forms the grain. Now, a part of this nitrogen content is under the control of the grain grower himself. In order to have a good supply of nitrogen, or protein, which is practically the same thing, in the kernel, it is necessary to have a good supply in the land. An experiment was carried on in Reno county, Kansas, some years ago, along these lines: Grain was taken that had been grown on a piece of land from which grain crops had been continuously taken for years, as we are now doing in western Canada. By the side of it was a sample taken from land that until five years previously had for several years-I do not know how many -been growing alfalfa. Alfalfa, sweet clover and other leguminous crops gather nitrogen from the air and store it up in the soil, where it is available for the grain. What were the results? The grain grown after alfalfa proved to have 14.36 per cent protein, while the grain grown a few rods away on land where there had been continuously growing grain had only 11.72 per cent protein. In addition to that, the alfalfa land gave a much heavier crop. So it is apparent that farmers can to a large extent control the amount of strength or protein in their grain.
Under our present system there is no encouragement to the grower to improve the quality of his grain. One party may be growing grain of a weak and soft variety that is lowering the general average of our grain on the markets of the world; the other may be doing those things that are necessary to produce a strong grain, such as growing it on high land, cultivating his land early in the season, using a stronger variety of seed and growing the crop in rotation, so that he has always a plentiful supply of nitrogen in the soil. Yet under the present system there is no inducement offered the farmer who does this. It is found in western Canada, and also in Dakota and other parts of the United States, that land that has been growing grain continuously year after year is now producing much poorer samples and the grain is bringing a lower price in the markets of the world. Notwithstanding this fact we have a system that does not in any way encourage the growing of better grain.

I follow that up by pointing out why it is that frequently the shrunken wheat, the wheat that is low in weight per bushel, is of -more value. The protein is the first element that goes into the kernel ; later on comes the starch. Now, if anything occurs to impede or stop the growth or filling of the kernel the protein is already in the kernel, but the starch does not get there; that is, the last element that goes into the kernel is the starch. Every day near the end of the ripening season when the kernels are bulging and becoming larger it is because of the starch finding its way into the kernels. Accordingly if you check the maturing of grain several days before it is finished you have a higher percentage of protein and a lower percentage of starch. That is the quality the millers want; when they buy a bushel of wheat not fully matured they are getting a larger percentage of the valuable protein, and yet under our system that wheat-is classed away down and has to take a very low price.
Some have taken objection to this system of handling grain because they say it wiil

take a long time to make the tests and will tie up the grain at the inspection points. Let me point out that there are different systems under which this principle is adopted. In Kansas they have perhaps the most perfect system of handling grain on protein content of any place on the continent. Kansas has its own system; Dakota has its own system; Nebraska has another system, but the system in Kansas seems to be the best. I am speaking now of the pool in Kansas. The system there is to draw a sample of grain at the elevator when the load is delivered. That sample is drawn by the farmer and the elevator operator and sent to their own laboratory in the city. A test is made and the results are then sent to the head office, where each individual shipper has his own account; his name is attached to the sample and the results of the test are transferred to his account. You can see how they have created a system which gives each individual grower the full value of his wheat. If he sends in a 16 per cent protein sample that result is transferred to his account in the head office, and in this case he receives returns in the course of eight or ten days according to the protein content of his wheat.
Then there is the question of premiums; they are paid a premium of from one to two and one half cents for every quarter of one per cent. That means at least four cents for every additional percentage of protein. Is that worth while? Following that, 1 might state t hat the systems adopted in Dokota and in Montana are somewhat similar. They frequently buy individual cars, and pay a premium. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) a short time ago instanced a case where two samples of grain were sent from Canada to the Minneapolis mills. Although according to our Canadian system the two samples graded the same, and the farmer received the same price, on the Minneapolis market one sample received twenty-six cents per bushel more than the other. They handle the grain in that way; they pay premiums for individual cars, but they also have a system of paying premiums to stations. A certain station in Montana is found to produce wheat high in protein content, say fifteen per cent. In that case they pay a premium of fifteen cents or sixteen cents for all the grain coming from that station. Recently a friend of mine had a letter from his brother in Montana, in which he said that on all his grain he had received a premium of sixteen cents per bushel. In Nebraska we find a somewhat

Supply-Trade and Commerce
similar system; they are classified in stations. Here is a shipping station handling grain of twelve per cent protein content; another ships grain of thirteen per cent protein, and they are spoken of in that way. The premium is also paid in that way; all the grain from the thirteen per cent station will receive a higher premium than that from a station with an average of only twelve per cent.
I mention these points to show that in the United States it has not been found impossible to overcome these difficulties. They have faced these obstacles that have been raised in Canada year after year as a reason why we should not adopt this system of grading and selling grain, and they have been overcome. I might read a paragraph from the same delegate quoted a few moments ago, Mr. Cox of Kansas. He is speaking now of the pool which handles grain in this way, and says:
Our growers never knew much about that,-
Speaking of the protein.
-until the pool started. The fact is that the 10,000 growers in the Kansas pool are the only farmers in Kansas who can receive the benefit of their actual protein up to the present time, through their own association. It is impossible for a grain man to g'.ve exactly what it is, when in the country, because he has no way of testing it. We own our own laboratory and our growers take a sample with the elevator man of every lot of wheat, and it is sent to our own laboratory. We run the protein and send that test to .the head office, there we have an individual account with every grcwer and put down exactly the protein he is entitled to. Then we get grades from him and the elevator man at the time of delivery, from the wheat ticket. The sample goes to the laboratory and back to the office and in that way he gets credit for the protein and at the end of the year he is settled with according to grade and protein.
I am not suggesting for a moment that we should do away with our present grading system, but I do think that protein should be a factor as well as weight and colour, neither of which indicate the actual strength of the wheat. You can see that under our Canadian system it would not be necessary to hold up cars at Winnipeg; samples could be drawn at the country elevator and sent to the laboratory at Winnipeg, and the results could be recorded in the head office.
The question was asked as to how the pool protects itself against fake samples being sent in. The delegate pointed out that the pool has a contract with the elevator men to supply the same grade of wheat and wheat of the same strength as he receives. Therefore they are bound1 in self-protection to see that a fair sample is drawn and submitted to the laboratory.
Another objection has been made to this system of handling grain, and that is that when you get the quantity of protein, it does not indicate the quality. In a letter that came to me a few days ago, a British writer pointed out that this is not very important. In the case of grain that is damaged, once a buyer would see damaged grain, or grain that was frosted, or with green kernels or anything of that sort, he would not ask for the protein test, because it would be of little or no value, but it is of value in the higher grades. In a very large measure it indicates the value of the wheat in the higher grades. If that is the case, why would it not be wise to assist the pool? I believe that the time has come when this is a problem, not for the government, bqt for the pool, and I discuss it at this time because when the pool undertakes to handle the grain in this way, the support and assistance of the government will be necessary, and changes will be necessary in the Grain Act providing for the handling of grain.
We find that in the States the custom of handling the grain in the elevators is to classify the grades having about the same protein content, and put those grades in the same bin. It may be that it will be found wise to take No. 2 grain and mix it in some cases with No. 1. That is a matter for the elevator men and the grain handlers to work out. They have worked it out in the United States, and there seems to be no reason why we could not work out such a system here. But it will necessary to have considerable changes made in our handling system. That has been one of our difficulties in adopting this method of handling grain because, as has been pointed out, after the test was made, if it was found that certain grain was high in protein strength, it would be difficult to maintain the identity; it would take too much space. I am not sure that that is the case; in fact, it would seem from the information that comes to me from the states of the union, they store wheat of the same protein strength in the same bins. It would seem that it is not found expensive; it is satisfactory; they are adopting the system, and their officials state quite freely that it has come there to stay. Here is the reason why it has come to stay.
The large millers have been forced in past years, both in Canada and the United States, to sell flour from grain that has been brought up to a standard of about 12 per cent protein. It was pointed out by one of the delegates attending the convention of which I spoke

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that three carloads of grain, one of 14 per cent protein, one of 12 per cent, and another of 10 per cent, ground separately, produced flour of a different quality from three carloads of grain all of about the same strength, and the bakers have demanded of the millers that they supply them constantly with a blend or patent of flour that is of about the same strength, and the millers are doing that. In some cases, in fact, the millers have made long contracts for months ahead for large quantities of flour, guaranteeing its protein strength. That has forced them to search for the high protein wheat.
Another objection raised to this method of handling grain in Canada is that we have not a market for it, _that there is not the demand for it, that we could not get any considerable premium. It does not seem to me that that Objection is well taken. At the present time the American buyers are buying our high protein wheat in very large quantities, and taking it to the United States to grind for export. In this way they do not require to pay any duty on it. They pick out our choice cars of grain at Winnipeg and other points, and ship them to the United States, and our grain is there mixed with their soft wheat and with wheat low in protein content. If they desire our wheat now, as their land is becoming poorer with the constant cropping of grain, is it not reasonable to believe that in future they will require our grain to a greater degree, and that they will become keen competitors for our strong wheat? It is not necessary for them to pay the 42 cents duty. They can take our wheat in without that duty, and they are doing it now.
In the report of Dean Rutherford, a member of the Turgeon commission, who visited
England a couple of years ago, he states that certain millers there have said to him: We will pay a premium for this strong wheat if you can deliver it to us, that is, if it is worth your while to go to the expense of retaining the identity of the wheat and classifying all the strong wheat together. As is well known the large millers of Canada at the present time through their line elevators and also through picking out cars at Winnipeg, after inspection, are securing the very best of our wheat. They have samples sent in from different shipping points in Canada in the early part of the season, and they find out at what points the strong wheat is being grown. It is not always at the same points. A point that grows strong wheat this year may not do so next year. Now if our millers are taking these measures for securing our strong wheat, is there any reason to believe that if our government would establish a laboratory to take care of the samples that are sent there, and would make protein tests and deliver to the grower a certificate, the same as they do now with respect to grades, the system would not be a success? I have in my possession the inspection cards that are used in Kansas by the laboratory making the tests. If our government would make tests and deliver to the grower a certificate showing the protein strength of his wheat, it would be about as far as they could go. It would then be left to the trade and to the pool to establish a system whereby the farmer would be able to receive a premium for his grain that was strong in protein content. I shall not detain the committee any longer. While it is uphill work to get the people convinced that this is a proper method of handling grain, the only way to get what you want is to keep pounding away, and I have studied this matter sufficiently to be convinced that it would be an advanced step. I do not expect, after we have discussed the matter in this way, that we shall immediately have the system of -grading grain changed, but I am in hopes that the government will see that its laboratory at Winnipeg is enlarged and made capable of making all the tests that are required. Some may ask, how long does it take to make a test? It requires from one hour to one hour and a half. What is the cost? In the United States and in the laboratory at Winnipeg the cost varies from 40 cents to one dollar, so the -cost is not excessive. Those who find that their wheat is low in protein, low in strength after having had a test made of one car probably would not care to have tests made on other cars. But it gives an opportunity to the man who is doing his best to keep his land up, to keep up the nitrogen strength, of his wheat, to produce wheat from the strongest varieties-in a word to grow wheat of the very highest type. That gives him an opportunity to earn a premium on that wheat that will pay him for his effort, and that is the least I believe that can be done. As I pointed out before, it is not encouraging to devote one's efforts to producing the best

stagedirection
speechtext: wheat, wheat that is worth in extreme cases 50 cents a bushel more than the wheat of the same grade of one's neighbour, when it fails of recognition. The premium mentioned is probably the maximum when .you take the premiums that are sometimes paid on the American market. It is not likely that we shall reach the same premium on the Canadian market, for a time at least. But in extreme cases a premium of 50 cents a bushel has been paid; in other cases it would amount to 10, 15 or 20 cents. That figure would be common. It is therefore not encouraging to a man not to be rewarded 'by this premium after all the .efforts he has put forth. It is all very well for some people to say: You believe in pooling; why not pool?- I believe in pooling where it is necessary, but we do not usually think it is wise to go so far in the case of horses as to pool a horse that is worth $200 with a Scrub thlat is only worth $50. On the same principle we do not believe iit is in the interest of the grain trade nor in the interest of the farmer himself to deprive him of the premium to which he should be entitled when he enhances the value of his grain.

I know the
minister is anxious to get his estimates through and I shall occupy only a few minutes in what I have to say. First of all let me state that I concur in the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle

Supply-Trade and Commerce
(Mr. Millar). I was not in my seat when he began to speak, but I presume his remarks were to the effect that he wishes the laboratory at Winnipeg to be enlarged in order to carry on to a much greater extent the testing of grain. It may not be a convenient opportunity to occupy the time of the House but I am impressed by the fact that the people in western Canada, possibly the people in Canada as a whole, are interested in the production of good grain, especially wheat. That is why the question at issue Should continue to be agitated until some action is taken to improve our system' of grading wheat. We have often heard the statement "Pigs is pigs" and many people when they think of wheat entertain the idea that "Wheat is wheat"- that whether you have a 60 pound sample or a 48 pound sample of wheat the quality is very much the same, and that it is merely a matter of pounds. But that does not necessarily follow. Even in the case of one field of wheat part summer fallow and part spring ploughing, both may grade the same, but there may be a great difference in quality since part of it may have a greater protein content and so be worth more money. Just as in the case of every other line of business, the farmer who is engaged in growing wheat should be encouraged to produce better wheat and to compete with others in doing so. If he is not given the necessary encouragement it all comes back to a question of looking at wheat simply as wheat without regard to the difference in value. Sometimes wheat is discoloured and yet it is possible that nothwith-standing that discolouration its quality has not been injured in the least. I had not expected that a discussion on this question would have arisen to-day, otherwise I would have equipped myself with certain data which I do not happen to have with me owing to the question having arisen so unexpectedly. I point out, however, that baking tests have been made by the government of different varieties of wheat, some of them discoloured to different degrees. In the case of the discoloured varieties it was found that when ground into flour it had not lost in any way its breadmaking or protein value. I believe in the results of these tests because they were carried out in a scientific way. The trouble with the present system of grading is that in too many cases it is unscientific. A man will come along, pick up a handful of wheat, and say that the grade is so-an-so. We all know that there is a difference in value even in the same grade of wheat, when graded under our present system. When the grading of wheat is carried out in a scientific manner the best grades 
realize a premium varying in amount. I believe we should do our utmost to encourage the wheat grower to earn a premium by producing the best varieties. There should be joint action by business men, millers, and agriculturists to continue the agitation for a better method of grading until success finally rewards their efforts. The objection is often heard that you cannot have a scientific system Of grading owing to the volume of wheat grown. This is only an argument to set aside the case. We do not know whether any plan is feasible or not until we have tried it. I hope the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who has studied wheat all his lifetime, will eontinue< his efforts until he succeeds in having a better system of grading adopted. He will always have my support. Grading is being improved in the case of eggs, butter, cattle and hogs; why should improvements not also be made in wheat? The present system of grading is obsolete and there should be no let-up in the agitation to improve it.

speechtext:
Before the item passes I wish to make some observations in reply to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. They have brought up a subject of great interest not only to the grower of wheat but also to the purchasers, particularly to the milling industry of Canada. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle knows quite well that the milling value of the crop varies from year to year. Climatic conditions have something to do with it, and while a few years ago particular parts of the country were noted for the wheat of excellent milling value they produced, my hon. friend knows that within recent years the Canadian millers, who have trained chemists who conduct scientific tests into the value of grains grown in different localities, have practically boycotted some of these districts. I am glad that my hon. friend has brought this question up. It will direct the attention of the grain grower to the importance of selecting wheat of high protein value and of keeping away from those grades of wheat that are practically boycotted by the Canadian miller although they are used in some foreign countries. I am glad my hon. friend has emphasized the importance of careful cultivation and of following a rotation of crops so as to preserve the protein value of the wheat in the highest degree. But even

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that may be impossible under certain climatic conditions. I recall that a couple of years ago I was shown confidentially a chart of certain sections of the country where it was pointed out that the wheat was of a very inferior milling quality, showing that there was very little protein value in the wheats of certain sections. I have before me a record of the conditions in Kansas, so much referred to by my hon. friend. The average protein value of Canadian wheat is higher than the average protein value of Kansas wheat. There are certain wheats grown in Kansas of higher protein value than others. I am not proposing to tell the growers of wheat what grain they should grow but my hon. friend knows that within recent years in some sections of the country they have put in Durum wheat. The number of bushels have been considerably more to the acre, but they have not convinced the man who uses it that the Durum wheat is of the same value as the other wheat, and you must not run away with the idea that the man who grows wheat of good protein value does not get the benefit, or that the quality is not recognized by the Canadian millers, because they always pay a premium for that kind of wheat. They have buyers out spotting, and they pay a higher price for it. I have nothing to say against the point urged by my hon. friend. I am quite in sympathy with the idea of keeping up the highest possible protein value of our Canadian wheat, and I go a step further and say that there should be a system of enabling the grower of the wheat to get, without much cost, a record as to the protein value of his wheat. I do not think it is under any state inspection in the United' States, but my hon. friend knows that in Kansas they get that protein value. The protein value is established through machinery in the agricultural college of Kansas where the testing is carried on.

There is one state where
they have state inspection for protein.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may have it in some of the states, but in the agricultural college they keep a record of it, and that is what I am alluding to. I understand that in the Research Council, of Which Dr. Tory is the chairman, they have made arrangements with the Board of Grain Commissioners to appoint a committee specially to advise with the Board of Grain Commissioners with reference to an improved method of establishing the protein value of Canadian wheat, and if there is not sufficient in the main estimates we propose to put something in the supplementaries to provide for this undertaking.

I should like to say a word about the grading of wheat. I recall a portion of an article written by the late Goldwin Smith a good many years ago, and I think what he said would apply to the situation. He said, "I know books because I am able to test them as a cheese monger can test cheese". The cheese mongers used to have a little auger and they bored into the cheese, then they took the auger out and smelled 5 p.m. it, and they were able to say, "that is so and so, such a grade". I think the cheese monger's test applies to our wheat. I think the minister rather outlined it when he said the conditions were changing every day in regard to the grading of wheat. It may be a climatic or other dhange. There are a lot of contributing causes which vary every year apparently in the growing of wheat, and in some way the men who buy the wheat have the same method of testing as the cheese monger. A buyer can tell in a second what the grade is. But the grade is not permanent as to content, protein or anything else. It is subject to change according to the climate. Something happens in connection with the seed; it varies with the years, and a product such as wheat is never permanent, but is influenced by the change of climate. There is some kind of internal development, so far as I can gather, in connection with the products of all kinds of growth and the process changes. It is all right to have experts in the schools of agriculture and to employ chemical analysis to ascertain the real qualities for the purpose of grading wheat. I do not know where it is going to end, I think every credit should be given to Dr. Tory and those who are trying to solve the problem, but the outstanding feature is that the ordinary buyer has the ability to grade the wheat in a moment. We ought to be able, in connection with our agricultural and other schools, to produce men who instinctively possess the faculty of being able to grade wheat, to fix its value and to say whether it will meet the demand of the foreign market. That market knows what it wants. They are always on the look out and they have the nose for buying. I am not a farmer, but I have heard a lot of this discussion. Perhaps I am not contributing anything to it, but the outstanding feature is the gift of the grain buyers, and these are the men who will make the greatest contribution to the problem of grading our wheat.
