Mr. Chairman, under
the previous item we had some discussion about the elevator at Prince Rupert. In my constituency we feel we were discriminated against when that elevator was not built on the Fraser river at or near New Westminster. The case for the Fraser river has been presented on many occasions. I remember a number of years ago when it was a matter of choosing between Vancouver and New Westminster for the construction of the first elevator, the Board of Grain Commissioners held a meeting at Winnipeg where the relative advantages of the two ports were presented to them. There were of course merits on both sides, and after a long discussion it was decided that the first elevator should be built at Vancouver. It was regarded more or less as an experiment. At that time I am informed a promise was made-not by the Board of Grain Commissioners of course-to the people of New Westminster that the next grain elevator on the Pacific coast would be constructed on the Fraser river.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What year was that promise made?

I think in 1912. A Conservative government was then in power. At that time the heads of the two great transcontinental railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern, favoured the location of elevators on the Fraser river. As a matter of fact, about that time the Canadian Pacific company purchased a large tract of land at Port Coquitlam on the Pitt river, a tributary of the Fraser river, for the purpose we were told of constructing, among other things, grain elevators. Subsequently the Canadian Pacific Company changed their policy and I think to-day they are practically out of the elevator business altogether. The Canadian Northern acquired Port Mann on the Fraser river just above New Westminster, it being their intention to build grain elevators there. As I have said, both railway

Supply-Trade and Commerce
companies favoured 'the Fraser river for that purpose. Why? Well, the minister has been out to the Pacific coast a number of times, and I remember on one occasion he visited New Westminster and met a number of the leading people there, who presented to him the advantages of the Fraser river in regard to elevator sites. The minister, I think, was quite impressed-at least he told us so at the time, and I believe he is always sincere.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did he promise an elevator?

As a matter of fact I think he did promise them an elevator some time; he would not tie himself down to the exact time when that elevator would be built. But the Fraser river, as the minister very well knows, possesses certain advantages for this purpose. I have no doubt he appreciates the fact that the Fraser river at or near New Westminster is the closest point at which grain from the prairie provinces can be transferred to ocean-going vessels. He also knows that all the grain that comes over the Canadian National Railways must first come to Port Mann and New Westminster. The minister has been told a number of times, and I think must realize, that there would be a saving to the Canadian National Railways of $13 a car on all grain coming over that line if it was taken off the cars at Port Mann instead of being carried over to Vancouver. The distance is not great, it is true, but those cars have to go across the bridge at New Westminster and pay a toll to the provincial government, and as the Canadian National tracks stop ait that bridge, their cars have	to	be transferred	to the GreatNorthern tracks to be taken over to Vancouver, where they have again to be transferred	to	the	Canadian Pacific tracks andswitched to the elevator. That means of course that those cars have to await the pleasure of the Canadian Pacific, to a certain extent, and it is only human nature, and so works	out	in	practice, that	the CanadianPacific	handle	the Canadian	National cars
after they have attended to their own. Consequently there is a good deal of congestion in Vancouver owing to the limited trackage which is available there. That limited trackage was one of the principal reasons why the Canadian Pacific Railway Company desired to have grain elevators located on the Fraser river. All that switching means money; there is a saving of $13 per car to the Canadian National Railways on all grain sent to Port Mann instead of carried on to Vancouver. There is the element of time to be considered also, and I am told it takes as long to get 
these cars from Port Mann to Vancouver, because of all this switching, as to bring them from Edmonton to Port Mann.
There is another question, that of sites. I suppose in Prince Rupert it was necessary to buy a site. I do not know whether the cost of the site is included in the $1,200,000, but on the Fraser river it is not necessary to buy sites; the government already have four miles of sites at Port Mann. They have quite a large piece of property at New Westminster; altogether in New Westminster they have properties which cost the Canadian Northern Railway over $1,000,000. They also have another site half a mile in length at Woodward's landing, lower down the river near the gulf, so the sites are already there and will cost nothing. Then the question arises as to whether these sites are desirable, and if they are suitable for the construction of elevators. The minister has probably seen the Howe report; if he has not seen it, I will furnish him with a copy. The city of New Westminster secured Mr. Howe, one of the best elevator engineers in America, to report on the sites on the Pacific coast near Vancouver, including Burrard Inlet and the Fraser river. Mr. Howe reported that three sites on the Fraser river were suitable in every way for elevator construction, so there can be no question as to the suitability of these sites.
The next point is the channel. Have we a channel at New Westminster sufficiently deep to enable ships to come to that port? If the minister had been in the House last night when the Public Works estimates were being reviewed he would have heard the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) say that we now have in the Fraser river at the shallowest point a channel twenty-seven feet deep. This minimum depth only exists at two places, Woodward's slough and at the mouth of the river. The minister said that certain work is proceeding now which he is satisfied will, in a comparatively short time, result in the deepening of the channel at these two points to thirty feet, which will give a thirty foot channel from Port Mann to the gulf. That channel, even at twenty-seven feet, is sufficiently deep to handle almost any of the vessels carrying grain in those waters. As a matter of fact last year, as the Minister of Public Works told us, 150 deep sea vessels entered and left that port safely. We are shipping out large quantities of lumber to all parts of the world; we are accommodating all the ships carrying lumber from British Columbia ports, including a great many of the Canadian Government

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Merchant Marine boats. We have a number of these ships calling there regularly, so this would mean an increase in the business of that line.
Another advantage is the cost of construction. It is well known that the cost of construction on fresh water is much less than on salt water, due to the fact that in fresh water there are no teredos. The minister and hon. members of this committee know what teredos do to wooden construction, and as a result of that damage it is necessary in salt water to put in concrete construction, which is very expensive. In the Fraser river we have no teredos, however, and pile construction will last almost indefinitely, so the cost will be much less.
The remaining point is, would the grain come there; would there be business for an elevator if one were constructed on the Fraser river? I think it is admitted that grain has just started to flow out through Pacific ports, and the time will come when the present elevators in Vancouver cannot expeditiously handle the grain coming there; perhaps that time has already arrived. There is a necessity now for the construction of another elevator, and that elevator should be built on the Fraser river. At one time, as I have mentioned, there was a contest between Vancouver and New Westminster in regard to elevators; there was a time when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) championed the cause of Vancouver as against the Fraser river. He succeeded on that occasion but last year in this House he advocated Port Mann and 'the Fraser river for the construction of elevators.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member is in his seat now and says "hear, hear," so you will see that the feeling which at one time existed is no longer in evidence, and the people on the Pacific coast in the vicinity of Vancouver and New Westminster are all agreed that the Fraser river is the suitable and logical place for the location of further elevators.
I do not wish to say anything against any other part of British Columbia or any other part of Canada, but I do think there is no reason at all why the Fraser river should be longer overlooked. I believe I voice the sentiments of my constituents, altogether irrespective of their political tendencies, when I say that New Westminster has not been fairly treated in regard to elevators. The question may well be asked as to why private elevators have not been constructed on
the Fraser river. That is a reasonable question and one which must be answered. In Vancouver it was necessary first to have a government elevator; no private elevators were constructed there at all until after the Dominion elevator was constructed and proved to be a success. The same is true of the Fraser river; there is no elevator there yet. Let the government construct an elevator on the Fraser river, and I have no doubt that it will be successful and others will follow. If the minister has any doubt about that, I would refer him to the Minister of Public Works who will tell him that he is firmly convinced that an elevator on the Fraser river will be successful from the start. I say this, that if that elevator which was constructed at Prince Rupert had been constructed at Port Mann instead, it would have been used to its fullest capacity right from the start, and there would not have been the condition which prevails in reference to Prince Rupert. The House was told about the Fraser river before that elevator was constructed, and many of my friends to my left stood up in their places and told the government that the elevator should be constructed at Port Mann instead of Prince Rupert. They said then, and I repeat it now, that an elevator built at Port Mann would be used to its fullest capacity all the time. There is need for it, and it would be successful. There is not an argument that can be adduced on the other side that has anything in it at all. I am not going to worry about this elevator at Prince Rupert. The fact that the government had to lease it to the pool for $100 a year, after having advertised for grain which did not come to it, is sufficient to prove that ilt would have been better to have had that elevator on the Fraser river. If the minister wishes to help the Canadian National Railway, if he wishes to help the grain trade, if he wishes to avoid a situation such as at present exists at Prince Rupert, he will see to it that the next grain elevator is constructed on the Fraser river, on one of the sites which the government already have there.

The hon. member for Neiw Westminster touched on one point which I should like to mention. I do not see any reason why my hon. friend should not have his elevator, or two or three elevators for that matter, because this government builds elevators in various places and leases them for a nominal figure afterwards. I have here the lease which was made for the use of this Prmce Rupert elevator by the wheat pool. The elevator was built at a cost of $1,350,000,

Supply-Trade and Commerce
in round figures, and this elevator the government have leased to the pool for $100 a year. I have no quarrel with the pool; I have nothing to say against it; I think it showed good business instincts in getting the elevator at that figure, but it is an extraordinary proceeding for a government to go out of its way to build an elevator at Prince Rupert, which is 2,50 miles farther from the grain fields than is Vancouver, and then, having built it, never use it-not one bushel has gone through that elevator, except one carload just to test the scales-and then turn it over to the pool for $100 a year. The interest on $1,350,000 at '5 per cent would amount to about $70,000 a year, so there is a straight gift to the pool of the interest charge of between $60,000 and $70,000 a year. I find by the lease that the government have not only rented this elevator to the pool at $100 a year, but they practically guarantee to keep it in repair. I do not know that it takes in all repairs, but here is one clause:
The lessor will turn t>he said demised premises over to the lessee, together with all buildings, erections, machinery and fixtures in good and substantial repair, working order and condition, and that if it be found later that any expensive or major repairs-
Apparently the pool is to be permitted to make the minor repairs:
-are required owing to faulty erection or construction of the said elevator, the lessor hereby agrees to repair for the proper and successful operation of the said elevator, (but nevertheless the minister shall be the sole judge of the lessor's liability hereunder.
Then I notice another clause protects the pool in regard to fire, If the elevator should he touched by fire, lightning, tempest, flood or any other act of God the govemlment agrees to return to the pool the balance of the $100.
There are a number of other interesting clauses. I do not wish to take up the time of the House discussing this further except to say that I think it is a most extraordinary proceeding for the government to build! an elevator out of the line of the wheat tnade altogether at a cost of almost $1,350,000, and then lease it for $100 a year. I do not wish to criticise my hon. friend from Prince Rupert; he naturally is looking after the interests of his constituency. But I am criticising a government that is so careless of the interests of this country that it will1 take such a course as that. Everybody knows what it was done for. That elevator was built for no other purpose than to bribe the people of that constituency to vote for my hon. friend. Again I repeat, I am not 'criticising my hon. friend. He, like my good friends to my left and myself, is anxious to look after his constituents, but I
[Mr. Manion.l
certainly think such a course by the government is open to condemnation by this House. I would also point out that this lease provides that the elevator may be operated! as a private or public elevator, whichever the pool desires. They may make it a mixing house, or do anything they like with it. This is just an illustration, and there lare many of them, of the unnecessary extravagance of this government, and it is just another reason why the people are compelled to pay such high taxation today. I believe in helping the pool in every way, if it is a good thing, and the farmers think it is, but I do not think they should ask or should get a 'bonus of this kind to carry on the grain business at Prince Rupert or at any other place in this country.
The hon. member said that only one 'carload of grain went through that elevator at Prince Rupert. Then does he think it fair to say that the government made a gift of $75,000 to the pool?
I am not criticising the pool at all. I think they made a good business deal. They apparently wanted the elevator, or they would not have leased it.

I am sure my hon. friend
wishes to be fair to the pool-
And to the government too.
This is the question I wanted to put to him: Does he not think it wall cost the pool something to use that elevator? Would the elevator have been used at all if it had not been leased to the pool?

Probably not, but the pool evidently wiants an elevator there, or it would not have leased it, and if It wanted one it would have co^b about a million and a half to build it. So that the people of Canada are practically bonusdmg the pool to the amount of sixty or seventy thousand dollars, which represents the interest on that amount.
My hon. friend does not suggest that the pool would build an elevator there.

I would not. I am not
criticising the pool at 'all.
Is it not a question whether the pool will be able to make much use of it?
I should think so.

If they cannot use it, they
are not getting any gift of $70,000.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I agree with that, and it probably will not be used much, because to send wheat through the Primce Rupert eilevator you have to send it 250 milies farther by rail that it would have to go via Vancouver.
It is not 250 miles it is 167 miles.
I thought the distance was 250 miles.
You are. wrong again.
There is no "again" to it. The eilevator was built so that my hon. friend would get votes, and he got them.
I got them in 1917 too, without the etevator.

When this elevator has
been standing there another year or two and does not handle any grain, my hon. friend may not get the votes next time.
We will eee.
I agree with my hon. friend from Macleod that the wheat will not go over this route, and that is affl the more reason for criticising the government for making this expenditure of nearly $1,500,000.
I wanted to suggest that the wheat would not go there unless the pool got the eilevator.
My hon. friend is backing up my criticism of the government and I thank him for it.

I want my hon. friend to be
fair. I ask him not to suggest that the government is making a straight present to the pool of $70,000.

I was not trying to be unfair to the pool. I was simply bringing to the attention of the people the facts with respect to the government's action. But I think they know most of these facts, and it is time the government realized they should not spend the people's money on hair-brained schemes of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly the hon. member for Fort William, criticize us for spending public money in the development of ports or in building elevators, I point out to them that they are paying a very poor compliment to the people of Fort William and Port Arthur because there are few places in Canada where the government have spent more money than they have at the places named. I would prefer to think that the people of Port Arthur
and Fort William could not be influenced by the spending of public money. I submit there is money in the estimates this year for expenditures at the port of Fort William.
There is none for Fort William.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does 013^ hon. friend claim that when we are spending money at Fort William we are bribing the people?
No, but I do claim that three-quarters of the grain of western Canada is handled at Fort William and Port Arthur whereas at Prince Rupert none is handled.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When my hon. friend puts up that argument-
I did not put up that argument as to elevators generally; I said it was applicable to this particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have heard the argument frequently that these expenditures are intended as bribes to the people of the constituency. In the case of the elevator at Prince Rupert we have leased it to the Alberta wheat pool at a rental of $100 for a period of three years.
Two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For a period of two years, and the pool have relieved the government from all expenditure of whatever kind excepting expenditure the necessity for which may develop in the course of the construction of the elevator. As to that, however, we have a guarantee from the contractor. The pool have taken over the elevator and by arrangement there is to be no taxation upon the property, so that the government will receive $100 net.
Some hon. .MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Wait a minute. The pool have taken over the elevator for a period of two years while the route as a grain-moving proposition will be tried out. The representations made to us are that the elevator will be filled before the end of that period. The development of the adjacent country, the gram from which will not go down to Vancouver, will require elevator capacity. The conditions at Prince Rupert may be compared to the conditions when the previous government in which my genial friend opposite (Mr. Rogers) was Minister of Public Works, and Sir George Foster, Minister of Trade and Commerce, put in an elevator at Vancouver and tried it out. What were the conditions

Supply-Trade and Commerce
in Vancouver? The government of that time did not receive even $100 in revenue. Each year the government of that period experienced a loss, it was $8,690.86 the first year, and $7,335.54 the second year.

Vancouver is a natural
place to have an elevator.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is only a matter of opinion. The people of Prince Rupert have a high opinion of their own port. It is only a case of a difference of opinion.
No, it is a case of freight rates.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I admit that the freight rates
have to be considered. My hon. friend spoke of a difference of 160 miles.
I said 250 miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That applies to the movement of grain eastward from Edmonton, but what about the possible traffic that will be developed along the Grand Trunk Pacific line, and along a line running northward from it, when people are settled in that territory? My hon. friend knows also that the trade with the Orient is increasing each year, and he will not say that Prince Rupert is farther away from the Orient than Vancouver is? Prince Rupert is nearer the Orient than Vancouver, and in view of all the conditions, the people of the district think there will be no great difficulty in filling the elevator.
I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The consent of the Minister of Finance is sought in the case of all these projects and he has to exercise extreme care. I admit that I tried to cut down some expenditure in which my hon. friend was interested.
Mr. MANION; What was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Some work going on around
the harbour.
My hon. friend is a little bit too quick in throwing out insinuations that he does not back up. He says I was interested1 in certain work. I ask him to state what I was interested in.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who is making this speech?

I do not know who is
making it; but I object to my hon. friend's
insinuations, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for New
Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) advocated the spending of money on elevators at Port Mann, pointing out that it costs $13 a car more to
[Mr. Robb.I
move grain up to the present elevator, and reminding me of what the Minister of Public W'orks said last night in connection with the depth of water in the harbour. My hon. friend says that he is supported by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Well, I shall direct the hon. gentleman's remarks to the attention of my colleagues, the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works, and if what the hon. gentleman has said is true I am sure the government will not be allowed to forget the advantages of that great port.
I rather resent the reflection indulged in by the Minister of Finance in a comparison he made between the elevator at Vancouver and the one at Prince Rupert.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Vancouver elevator had
to be tried out.

When I agreed to undertake the building of the elevator at Vancouver, the Panama canal was to be finished in a very short time. The elevator was undertaken and constructed in a very creditable manner. Then the war came on and delayed the transportation of wheat through the Pacific port.
There were slides into the canal which delayed its operation.

Everything militated against that route for a few years, but the statement read to-day by my hon. friend with respect to returns showed the justification for the building of that elevator. If the elevator is making half a million dollars a year it is a very creditable showing, and1 justifies the course pursued in erecting it at Vancouver.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the elevator was built before the Panama canal was finished?
Yes.

In what year
was it built?

It was built in 1914-15, I
think. In any event the Orient was always there.

And then my
hon. friend will remember the slides into the canal.

Of course the war conditions prevented shipments through the port of Vancouver at first, but I tell the Minister of Finance to-day that Vancouver would be doing a great deal more business were it not for the fact that, through the government of

Quebec, Montreal and Southern Ry.
which he is a member, a statutory freight rate has been fixed that militates against the port to a very serious extent. Take the people of Calgary. If they want to ship grain to Fort William, a distance of about 1,280 miles, they can do it for 15 cents a bushel. On the other hand if they want to ship to Vancouver, a distance of 600 odd miles, just about half the distance, they are charged 13 cents a bushel when they should only be charged 8 cents. If we are to have a legitimate statutory rate it should apply to all parts of the country similarly situated in equal degree; and if the [DOT]Vancouver elevator has not earned more than half a milion dollars a year it is due to the manner in which it is discriminated against by the statutory rate fixed by tihe railway commission under the direction of this government.

The Prince Rupert elevator never was a political elevator. Hon. gentlemen opposite always insist that this elevator was built for the purpose of influencing the elections and winning the seat. Let me repeat what I have said several times already in this House, that we never required any such subsidy in order to carry the elections in 1917 when the War Time Elections Act was in effect and was used for the benefit of hon gentlemen opposite. On the contrary, the people of Skeena stood solidly behind Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy of developing the country to be served by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. And in 1917, without the subsidy on that elevator, they cast their votes in favour of the Liberal candidate, and again in 1921 and in 1925. In connection with the construction of this elevator at the end of the Grand Trunk Pacific line, I may point out that the people of Canada have a tremendous investment in that railway. When it was taken over and administered by the Mackenzie and Mann people, who were the natural enemies of the Grand Trunk Pacific, it was natural that it should fall into disuse, and unless the people of Canada are prepared to spend a little more money at the end of the Grand Trunk Pacific and develop some traffic over that line, it will always show a great deficit. This government decided that that piece of railway was worth salvaging, that it was worth spending more money on, and in order to induce traffic over the line they decided to construct an elevator in Prince Rupert. The construction of that elevator will bring this fall a tremendous tonnage over that line. The trade with the Orient is developing and increasing all the time, and Prince Rupert is the logical port. Stress is laid upon the ill-treatment of Vancouver by the placing of the elevator in 14011-300
Prince Rupert. For the last two years there has been congestion in the port of Vancouver when the wheat movement was on. Hundreds of thousands of cars, sprinkled all along the way from the prairie to Vancouver have been held up because of congestion at Vancouver; because at that port they could not handle the traffic offered. Surely it is a dog in the manger policy for Vancouver and the Vancouver supporters who sit on the other side of the House to claim that even though Vancouver is congested with wheat, even though they are unable to take care of the wheat that is routed there no Other port should get the traffic. There is room on the Pacific coast for two ports. Prince Rupert has many natural advantages as a port and we have great aspirations for its future in that regard. Indeed it is bound to be a great port. Adjacent as it is to the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, it will meet the needs of a vast wheat growing area which could only be served by the construction of this elevator. Last year I was up on the shores of Francois lake and I saw growing there a crop of wheat the equal of any wheat grown in Canada. There are over a million acres of wheat land adjacent to the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway which could use this elevator. Its construction is designed to create traffic over the Grand Trunk Pacific line of railway and to open up and develop a wheat country which otherwise would not be developed.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
The House in committee on Bill No. 191 to incorporate Gatineau Transmission Company-Mr. Fontaine-Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to oppose this bill on legal grounds and as a matter of public policy.
Louder.

In dealing with the question of 'disposing of the water powers of the country "we have a trust", as Mussolini said. "A country does not belong to the people

who live in it to-day. It is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present, and a trust for the future." I am very much disappointed with the action of the government of Ontario. They claim they are making an agreement with the company based on this bill. I fear that the Hydro is through except as operating as a filling station for the International Paper Company and other branches of the United States trust. They are going to ask Ontario to build this plant and give it to them at the end of thirty years free of cost, paying the 115 rate to build this plant for the United States trust, instead of as in' Chippawa paying rates to build a power plant for Ontario itself to own forever. I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the Privy Council recently decided that this parliament cannot declare a work to be for the general advantage of Canada unless it affects the body politic of the whole country. This company should have gone to the province of Quebec for incorporation, for the bill does not affect the federal body politic at all. It might as well be contended that a candy 3tore on Sparks street is for the general advantage of Canada. We are trustees for the people of the whole Dominion, and I protest against this bill because, as I say, it is not for the general advantage of Canada. As a matter of policy we are just at the parting of the ways. In the election of 1921 the Liberal party charged that the Conservative party was the creature of the big interests. Well, who are behind the Gatineau Power Company which is seeking incorporation by this bill? The United States superpower trust.

Mr. Chairman, I would request that the hon. member either speak louder or come down to the centre of the chamber so we can hear what he is talking about. It may interest us, and if so we would like to know what he is saying. We can hear nothing at all while he remains in his present position.

I am discussing the principle of the bill at present, and I believe I am voicing the opinion of a large number of the people of Ontario and of the municipalities who have invested money in the Hydro system. Now, without their consent and without a vote of the people these Niagara contracts which have been entered into are to be treated as scraps of paper and they are to be compelled to take power from a privately-owned plant. I am not at all surprised at what has been done, because the late Sir Adam Beck had to put up a fight to save the water power of Ontario for the

Gatineau Transmission Company
people, and I am not surprised at Mr. Ferguson's act. I know of nothing he has ever done for the hydro-electric system, so it does not surprise me to see him linked up with this bill, compelling the Niagara municipalities to part with their power and give it to western Ontario and take in lieu thereof power from this American trust, privately-owned and operated.
This House should protect the municipalities of eastern Ontario, which have been stagnant for a great many years because of the lack of cheap light and power. It has been suggested that Hydro power be developed at Morrisburg, but this government will not pass the plans and allow the work to proceed In my opinion this undertaking will not work to the general good of Canada, but will be harmful instead. As I see it, the money will come from the American superpower trust across the border. Under section 5 the location of the head office is named, and under the next section the purposes and powers of the company are defined as follows:
The coimpany may-
(a)	for the purposes only of conveyirog and trans-mrtitinig and delivering electrical power or energy, construct, operate and maintain transmission and distribution lanes, systems and works over or below ground or water, and along, across or under watercourses, and for such purposes erect and maintain poles and towers and lay and maintain pipes, cables, wires and other conductors;

speechtext:
I want to
speak about the principle involved in the franchise to build the road to Red Lake, because I think all that mining country, and it is the most promising mining country in the world, ought to be connected up with the Canadian National railways. At present a new thing is happening. There is a great mining country in the township of Rouyn, in the province of Quebec, where great dis-

coveries have been made and the township is desirous of getting railway service. Apparently they could not get railway service by going direct to the Canadian National Railways, so a local company was incorporated to build a line from Amos southeasterly to Rouyn. That road is being built by an independent company, and a big bond issue is to be floated in connection with it. This is a new development in the way of building branch lines from the Canadian National railway, that is, first to incorporate a local company for the purpose of building the road, and then issuing a large block of securities, and then later on unloading them on to the Canadian National. My contention is that this road ought to be taken care of absolutely as a branch line of the Canadian National railway.
Then when we come to this Red lake proposition, which is an extension probably of one hundred miles of railway to be 'built by a private company, we notice that there is a great rush to incorporate this company. We are having promoters come here from all over to build railways into that mining country. I do not know how many more of these companies will come along, but I do know that the richest mining country in the world to-day is in the province of Quebec, in Ontario, and probably in Manitoba, and all of these mines will want to connect up with the Canadian National railway. The stand I want to take here to-night, and I am sure I shall be backed up 'by public opinion in Quebec, Ontario and [DOT]Manitoba, is that the Canadian National Railway ought to build all these lines if they are worth being built at all. They ought to be owned directly by the people, and my suggestion is this, instead of giving a franchise to these private companies, the Canadian National ought to build this line direct themselves from Amos to Rouyn, and then southwesterly to Cheminis on the boundary between Quebec and Ontario, where they would join up with the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, and once on the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway they could go north and west, via Kirkland lake and on west to a station called Westree on the Canadian National, on the Sudbury main line. In that way we will have the National Railway serving all that mining country in Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba instead of a lot of local companies. Here is the second company coming forward for a franchise, and I make the prediction that there will be at least ten of them coming along later. Now that ought to stop. The greatest mines in Canada recently were dis-

Red Lake Railway Company
covered, first of all, when nickel was found near Sudbury, and next the Cobalt silver camp. The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway was built-it is wholly owned by the province of Ontario-and then came the discoveries in Porcupine. That territory also is served by the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY

Yes, because the exploiters want it, and they, perhaps, would put a little silence round the National Railways. The point I want to make is that this is the greatest mining country in the world. Part of it is in Quebec, part in Ontario, and part in Manitoba. The province of Ontario has 200 miles of this country, and what the Canadian National ought to do is not only to build these lines but take over the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario line which is practically a paying proposition now. Then the people of Canada would own the railways in the greatest mining country in the world. All I say is in the meantime let these profiteers whoever they are, these exploiters, wait.
There is no reason why we should give them this charter if the road is not needed. It was not intended to serve the mining country, it was to serve the exploiters.
Mr. O'NEILL: What about the Gowganda camp, in which I understand my hon. friend is interested?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I am not interested in Gowganda at all.
Mr. O'NEILL: What you are saying has to do with its welfare.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
No, what I am anxious for is to see the greatest mining country in the world preserved for the National Railways. When the National line is up there it ought to have the opportunity to secure the traffic. Let me tell my hon. friend something. The National Railways get out a magazine every month which is distributed among their employees. In this is a little card asking the reader-who of course is an employee of the company

if he knows of any traffic that it is possible to get in his district, and if he does, to send to the head office a post card containing the information. That shows how anxious they are to get freight. They should be equally anxious to secure the railways that are going to develop the northern country. My contention is that the Canadian National should own the line from Amos right through Rouyn to Cheminis on the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario at the interprovincial line, through the Kirkland Lake gold field to Swastika, then north to Earlton Junction. Then west to the present terminal at Elk Lake, then on via Gowganda and Shining Tree to Wfestree on the Sudbury line, opening up the richest area in Quebec and Ontario of copper, gold, silver and gold again. That is the greatest series of lines through a mining country that I know of, and they can all be combined in one. That would be a profitable route and would give the Canadian National complete control of the territory. We have got the whole northern country now practically outside of the Canadian Pacific, that is at all profitable. I do not want to see any unnecessary rush in building railways. I do not know why parliament should let these other people go ahead before the National Railways have a chance at it. Of course the Minister of Railways says the Canadian National Railways have no present interest in the matter. Certainly not if the method is continued which has been followed in connection with the development of the Rouyn field, that is, to allow a local company to get a charter, issue securities to build a road, and then sell out at a great ad-

vance to the Canadian National Railways. The principle I have indicated is the general principle I have laid down here. If you grant the present request it will not be long before other people will be asking for charters for the construction of small lines to serve the mining country in Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was -replying, by way of defence of the Prince Rupert elevator, to the remarks that had been made by the hon. member (Mr. Manion) in which particular emphasis was laid on the fact that this elevator had been leased to the wheat pool at a nominal rental of $100 per annum. The hon. gentleman indulged in considerable criticism of the government on this account. Certainly $100 is a modest sum; but, as the minister pointed out, the wheat .pool in taking over the elevator takes over at the same time the payroll and all expenditures connected with its operation. When we recall the disastrous experience of the Vancouver elevator during the first two years it operated this rental of $100 a year -for the one at Prince Rupert will bear scrutiny. One of the last acts of the government of which my hon. friend from Fort William was a member for a few fleeting weeks was to provide for the construction in the city of Victoria of a dry dock at a cost of some $6,000,000. and I venture to say that if the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), to-day wanted to lease that dry dock, which will be completed this fall, he would not receive a bid of $100 if the contracting company had to assume all obligations in connection with its operation. I am in no way criticising the Victoria dry dock, for I am very grateful to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) for the assistance he gave us when the Prince Rupert elevator was under consideration in the House. The hon. member for Fort William would1 do well to observe, as I have always tried to observe, the old adage that bids us live and let live. The Victoria dry dock is just as liable to censure as is the Prince Rupert elevator, but I have noticed that those who are most ready to criticise the Prince Rupert expenditure know least about it. The hon. member for Fort William had a good deal to say about this matter in the last campaign, although he has never yet been interested enough to visit the country of the Grand Trunk Pacific, nor has he ever set eyes on Prince Rupert.

That may be true, but I
have visited the Grand Trunk Pacific country. I have not seen Prince Rupert, but that is not the whole of the western country.

It is an important part of
it.	.

In my hon. friend's
opinion.

I should be glad to have ah the opponents of the Prince Rupert elevator come out there and learn a little about their own country.

I appreciate the way
this government look after their friends. They look after them first, last and always; it is the first thing in the morning, it is the noontime meal and it is the evening meal. Then they try to justify it before parliament. I admire the astuteness and ability of the Min-

ister of Finance for the defence he put up this afternoon, but when you boil it down to the last analysis it is simply this: We have spent SI ,300,000 of the people's money to put an elevator at Prince Rupert in order that the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Stork) may retain his seat in this House. That is only one of the 245 constituencies represented in this House where the government has tried to debauch the electors in order that candidates supporting the government might be returned. Negotiations took place to debauch the constituency that II now represent and seduce the former member to desert the party to my left, which he was elected to support, and go over to the government. But I need not delve into further history of this kind. The people know all about it, they know this government in order to retain office is ready to secure support by any means within their power. The Prince Rupert elevator is an instance. They have used it to good advantage, I admit. The best evidence is that the hon. gentleman from Skeena is a member of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to
what the hon. member for Skeena has said respecting the dry dock at Victoria, I would point out to him the well-known. fact that in 1917 there appeared to be imminent danger of a German squadron attacking the Pacific coast, there was considerable excitement, and as a precautionary measure the provincia1 government purchased a couple of submarines. I happened to be in England when the matter came before the admiralty, and was sent for to discuss conditions on the Pacific coast, with the result that the admiralty refused to send a warship in there because there was no dry dock. The late Mr. Bonar Law, then a member of the British war cabinet, supported the request by the naval authorities that we undertake the construction of a dry dock at Victoria as rapidly as possible. The work was started and, as I understand, is now completed. As hon. gentlemen are aware, shortly after I came back to Canada 1 resigned, and since then I have not been in touch with conditions at the coast. I want my hon. friends to have no misgivings about the dry dock at Victoria. If it is not serving any useful purpose at the moment, it must not be forgotten that it was built at the direct request of the British government solely for military purposes.

I should like my hon. friend
to understand that I was in no way criticizing the Victoria dry dock.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, I want to get the committee away from this political discussion if I possibly can. It seems to me that the government should have under consideration the providing of additional drying facilities at our western terminals. We find in Alberta especially, for our grain feeds most of the terminal elevators on the Pacific coast, that we generally have different grades of wheat;-not always, but it happens very frequently-frosted, at other times damp. Last year much of the wheat was damp, and when in that condition it gives the transportation companies an excuse, sometimes necessarily so, when drying facilities are really inadequate, to put in effect what is known as the permit system, which means that grain intended for the Pacific coast must go eastj ward, where there are drying facilities. When the farmer ships his carload of wheat to the elevators he may not know whether it is damip or not; therefore the transportation companies take no chance, but say: This may be damp wheat, consequently you will have to get a permit. This system interferes very materially with the westward flow of wheat. Last year it was invoked and prevented the flow of our grain to the western terminals. I am not one who wishes or expects to see all our wheat go westward; I know it will go easward or westward, according to supply and demand. I think there is now fairly ample storage room at the terminal elevators, but the drying facilities are inadequate, and the government should see that these facilities measure up to the other accommodations. This is a very important item. All western men connected with the grain trade know that ample drying facilities must be furnished to take care of the regular flow of grain westward.
At what points?

At Vancouver or wherever the elevators may be. I should like to see elevators along the Fraser river. I wonder a private company does not invest capital there. The grain trade to-day is in a different position from what it was when the government built the elevator at Vancouver; it is now an established fact that a very considerable proportion of our grain goes westward, and will continue to go in increasing quantities, with proper elevator accommodation. I have no doubt that with elevator accommodation the Fraser river would get a lot of the grain before it reached Vancouver. Therefore I should like to see private elevators built there, and I would not object to the government giving assistance to this end. There certainly seems to be an inviting investment at that point as nearly as I can find out. But I do wish to urge upon the minister this one fact-I think he is aware of it already, for no doubt complaints have come to him-that we want some additional drying facilities on the west coast. I do not know what it would cost to provide these facilities, probably the capital outlay would be considerable, but if we provide the storage accommodation we must also provide corresponding drying facilities.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman is probably correct as to the field for private investment in elevators along the Fraser river, for that is the place where there is a demand for -the grain. He is perfectly right when he says the grain will go where the demand for it is. My hon. friend from Skeena gives us a reason to-day for the building of the Prince Rupert elevator-congestion at Vancouver. I think he said-if my recollection is wrong he will correct me-that some 100,000 cars of grain were held up at Vancouver. Is that right?
Yes, many hundreds of cars were on the road between the prairies and Vancouver.
I thought my hon. friend said 100,000.
No, I said many hundreds.

Therefore the reason we build at Prince Rupert is that there is congestion at Vancouver. We knew what the real reason was, always, but this is the first time we have got an avowed reason- this elevator is built at Prince Rupert because there is congestion at Vancouver. I should like to apply to that reasoning the common sense statement of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Tobin). Grain moves where it is wanted. That is the ordinary way about everything. But the real justification of this government for building an elevator at Prince Rupert, according to the member for Skeena, is: Because there is congestion at Vancouver, where facilities are required, we will build an elevator at Prince Rupert, where there is no grain going. That is the pitiful excuse we get to-day, but the one interesting thing is that this is the first time a real attempt has been made to present an excuse; the thing was so absolutely inexcusable. The hon. member was saying tha1 the Tories were calling this a political

Supply-Trade and Commerce
elevator. Two gentlemen who have been voting with the government all through this session stood up this afternoon and said that one of the shackles placed upon the grain trade of western Canada by this government was the building of political elevators, and this elevator at Prince Rupert was described as such by these two hon. members. They certainly did not idly so charge the action of the government they support; they said it because they know it to be true. Everyone knows it to be true, but some will not admit it.
I am also going to agree with a further remark made by the hon. member for Macleod (M>r. Coote). In reply to the hon. member for Fost Wil'liam (Mr. Manion) he pointed out that under the circumstances 'he did not think the hon. gentlleman was quite fair to the pool when he suggested that the pool were getting a whole lot for nothing. I do not think they are. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, in one sense they are getting a great deal1 more than they should get, because usually the last thing a government should do is give one concern an advantage over others; they should treat them all alike. For example, this government has elevators at other points in the system, and business elevators as contrasted with political elevators are rented for a return of 7 per cent of the investment. Here we have an elevator rented for $100, as against others rented on that basis of a return of 7 per cent. I will illustrate some of these cases, so there can be no dloubt about it. Let us consider the big elevator at Port Arthur, acquired by the government when the Canadian Northern system was taken over; that elevator is rented now to the Saskatchewan Co-operative. The Saskatchewan Co-operative is a first rate concern; it is operated similarly to the pool, by and for the farmers, and there is no reason why we should turn round and penalize the Saskatchewan Co-operative on the one hand and give property for nothing to the pool on the other hand. Nevertheless, we charge for that elevator a rental of 7 per cent of the value, and on the other hand we charge $100. Why? As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member for Macleod; the pool are not getting anything; they are trying a great experiment. They are now engaging in the task of trying to create a demand for grain where there is no demand; they are going to all' the expense and trouble of trying to work up a (grain business at a centre where no such business exists. There is no use rubbing it in; we all know that is what the pool' is trying to do. The grain commissioners have been running advertisements
[Sir Henry Dravton.l
in an attempt to get people to ship their grain where there is no demand for grain, and now the pool is going to try to do what the government has been unable to do. I only give this as an illustration. The other elevators are just the same, and I will say for the government that they have the same rate for everyone who wants business elevators. For instance, for elevator D, which is leased to a private 'company, 5 per cent of the whole capital' investment is received.
Will the hon. member tell me who built the external storage elevators at Moose Jaw and Saskatoon, and what return the government is getting from them?

I will have much pleasure an answering that question at once. These elevators' were built by a former Conservative administration; they are still maintained and operated by the government; they are not rented, but are some of the elevators which showed a profit.
What return are they making?

They are
among the elevators which showed a profit of something like $1,500,000 this year. They were put up for the purpose of this hon. gentleman who was speaking not very long ago about dry storage; they are for the purpose of looking after the crop at a time when elevators are necessary, and according to the record's they are very often necessary. Does my hon. friend suggest that these elevators are rented for $100 a year? If so he is wrong; they are not rented at all. They were put up for the western farmers and they are so operated.
Are you getting your interest on the money?

You had better ask the minister, who gave the figures this afternoon. This government thinks so much of the Moose Jaw elevator that at the request of the grain commissioners and on the motion of a gentleman from the district who knows something about it, Moose Jaw has been made an inspection point. Well, Mr. Chairman, I hope-and I trust the hope is not entirely vain-that we will not have any more experiments like this. Of course the hon. member will still go on talking in Prince Rupert; he says he wants if knocked here so he can go there and just tell the people what the wicked Tories would do. He can do a little more; he can go and tell them what two supporters of this govern-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
merit who know the business say of that elevator. He can go and say that the hon. member for Macleod and his friend describe it as a purely political elevator, but he will have to get- another tune. After all, vacant and idle elevators are not good assets; there are lots of honest ways of spending money profitably, and the sooner the hon. gentleman knows it is a bad thing not only for the country but for his own constituents to have money spent improperly, it will be better both for him and for his constituents.
Mir. TOLM'IE: We have heard northern British Columbia spoken of in a rather disparaging way by some hon. members tonight, and I would like to point out that there is a tremendous undeveloped empire in that northern country. It is well fitted for agriculture of a diversified nature and for the raising of cattle, and particularly dairying. I have never believed that we oan develop 800 miles of our Pacific coast by putting all the development into one harbour; I have always believed that we should divide it and give any place where there is an opportunity for development a chance to have some money spent in that direction. Whether or not this elevator at Prince Rupert will be a success is something that will be settled in the future. I remember quite well that when the elevators were built at Vancouver they were idle for some time. I remember that when it was proposed to build the Esquimau dry dock we were faced with the same kind of criticism we have heard to-night. Why was that dock built? A dock was built there in the seventies with a capacity of I think 434 feet; that is, no ship could be entered for repairs if it were longer than about 400 feet. During the war it was necessary for us to beg the United 'States government to permit us to send some of the British war vessels over to Bremerton, Washington, for repairs. Our -Canadian mechanics had to follow to the United1 States to secure work on the British ships. The new dry dock at Esquimalt which will be ready this fall for the accommodation of vessels is the second largest dock in the world. It will handle easily the largest ship 'in the world. It will take in the Hood without any difficulty whatever, and with from *one to two hundred feet to spare. It will take in at one time two large merchant vessels, or three smaller vessels. It is strictly [DOT]up to date in every possible respect.
. What have our American friends been doing in making provision for the quick repair of .ships on the Pacific coast? Before this Esquimalt proposition was undertaken in Canada, we had a little short dock in Esquimalt, and one other dock contemplated in the city of Vancouver, and at that very time the Americans had no less than sixteen docks scattered from the southern coast of California up to Puget Sound in the state of Washington, making every provision for the care of ships. With the development on the Pacific coast, the greater volume of commerce passing through the Panama canal, and the development generally of western Canada, this dry dock at Esquimalt will be an asset of the very greatest value to our shipping interests. We shall be prepared to handle any ship there, and handle it quickly. In looking over the whole of the Pacific coast for a spot at which to locate, Yarrow's Limited, the great shipbuilding firm of Glasgow, Scotland, decided to locate at Esquimalt. They are carrying on a large ship repairing business there, and also some shipbuilding. In one year alone they handled over 110 vessels in the small dry dock and on their slips, and they had to turn away many vessels because they were too large to be accommodated in the Esquimalt dry dock. I am quite sure that if the Minister of Public Works, who has charge of this branch of the government work, undertook to negotiate with any ship repairing firm, he could come to an agreement at once for the lease of that dock, but that would not be desirable because in connection with a government dock every ship repairing firm should stand on an equal footing and all be given an equal chance to secure the dock for that purpose. So the Esquimalt dry dock has a great future before it. It will only be a matter of a few years before the business of ship repairing will have increased to a very great extent on the Pacific coast. The building of that dock has been justified long ago, and the project will be endorsed by the development that will take place in the future. It is a very difficult thing to say at the present time, with the great development that is going to take place on the Pacific coast, just how an expenditure on any particular work is going to turn out until we have had a chance to see things develop, but we expect that Canada's great development in the future will take place on the Pacific rather than on the Atlantic for some years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before the item carries, may I say that provision has been made for additional driers at the Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Calgary houses? Vancouver is fairly well equipped, I think. I recall that in 1922 either myself or my predecessor, the hon. member

Supply-Trade and Commerce
for Vancouver Centre, gave a contract in connection with that house. It is fairly well equipped with driers, and they have been added to this year.

I would like to add a word to what the hon. member for Victoria has said with regard to that great north country extending down to Prince Rupert. It seems a shocking thing when one is reminded of an expenditure of $1,250,000 at Prince Rupert for an elevator, to think that practically nothing has been done to develop that great stretch of northern couritry in British Columbia. Some years ago I had the opportunity of traversing that section of British Columbia, and when one remembers that after you pass through the mountain pass you have practically 500 miles of country with hardly a mountain to be seen, and that nothing has been done to develop it, but that $1,250,000 has been thrown away on an elevator at tidewater at Prince Rupert, it seems to me it is only another evidence of the lack of business ability and acumen on the part of this government in failing to assist in the development of the natural resources of Canada. Why a half or a quarter of that money devoted to the assistance of a pulp mill, for instance, near Prince George would have provided employment there and enabled a settlement to have started. Another quarter of the money specifically set aside for settlement in that territory would have provided a great deal of traffic for the Canadian National lines. It does seem to me that in the expenditure of the capital funds of this country we ought to begin on a business basis and set aside certain areas in the nine provinces of the Dominion and work in co-operation with the provinces to develop traffic along the line of the Canadian National railway instead of spending money on useless projects such as this elevator at Prince Rupert.

speechtext: There is some difference of opinion, but not very much, as to this service. My hon. friend who has just spoken finds some fault with the vote. I recall when I was Minister of Trade and Commerce having a gentleman come in to see me who had just returned from a trip around the world. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will agree with that.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

It is thrown at this country because other countries that formerly would have been competitors with Canada in the foreign market are not now in a condition to compete. Therefore, as my hon. friend agrees, there is a very large increase in our foreign trade due to business which has been absolutely thrown at us. Our foreign trade is large and we are becoming more and more dependent upon it. Not only are we becoming more and more dependent upon the foreign trade having regard to our agricultural products, but we are also becoming more dependent upon that trade with respect to our industrial efforts. I have in mind a factory-I would not mind giving my hon. friend the particulars of it if he desires- that is very busy, and has been very busy for the last two or three years, possibly one of the few factories in Canada in that happy position. That is because it is in the export business. But the ordinary output of that factory was 80 per cent domestic and 20 per cent export. I may say that in the United States, which produces so many goods similar to what we do, and whose methods of life are so similar to our own, when their exports exceed 8 to 9 per cent of the total production it spells bad times -because their best market being their home market, the higher price is easily got at. But when the condition is the one I have mentioned, it means that the purchasing power is falling .off, and they look upon it as an indication of bad times. We have always exported more than they have. We have never been able to absorb as much of our own production as they have, our purchasing power not being nearly as great as theirs. But in connection with this factory the normal was 80 per cent absorbed by the purchasing power at home and 20 per cent exported. To-day only 40 per cent of that production is sold at home and 60 per cent is exported, not because we have gone into the business but simply because the competition we formerly had is non-existent. The business has been thrown at us, and we have fortunately been able to get it.
Is the total business of that factory more than it formerly was?

It certainly is. The hon. member will see the percentages. It would have to be bigger, or else they would be doing nothing in Canada at all, and while the Canadian business has shrunk, the total output is greater.

Mr .ROBB: What goods are they manufacturing?

Rubber tires. The reason is perfectly plain; before that the continental rubber tires hacf that market. They are not now in a position to finance raw material, the cost of which represents a large proportion of the finished article; so that we are doing very well in that business, as the hon. minister knows. I would much rather the government would spend money in connection with this vote than in connection with sonje others. I am now referring particularly to what they spent in connection with the arrangements made for treaties. The only place where we have been crimped in our export business is where we make trade treaties. I will stick to that same firm and give an illustration. Before we had our treaty with France that same firm had an office in France and was selling a certain amount of tires in France. As a result of the treaty we have to-day the ministers go over to the continent and negotiate for us, but this firm have had to close their office in France and cannot sell any tires there. Therefore I am anxious that any further effort for trade should be made upon business principles rather than upon the line of trade treaties brought about by very amiable gentlemen who have not very much knowledge of trade or business. The effect of that treaty with France is not confined to tires, because the result of the treaty is that last year we cut in two our exports to France, which were ascending before the treaty was made, and she doubled her sales here. This business is becoming vital to this country, and therefore we have to do something to hold this business which was thrown at us, or which we got as an accident. I hope my hon. friend will give the close attention which he at one time gave to this particular service. I will tell him that the service lately has not been satisfactory. He had a interregnum in his office as Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think when he was in office he took a fatherly interest in this particular branch of the service, and was interested in it, and I know that he had some good men; I ran across some very good trade representatives outside. But it has not been as it might have been for the last few years, and I hope my hon. friend will take -a real keen interest in it.

speechtext: That was in 1925. Mr. Clarke was sent down there in August, 1925, and succeeded in inducing the Greek government to remove the restrictions on patent flour, and during January, 1926, the restrictions on other grades of flour were removed entirely, and that was a very great advantage to Canadian trade.

The hon. member was dealing with Spain a moment ago. How is it that the trade returns in agricultural and vegetable products show that our exports to Spain, which in 1921 were $339,900, had decreased to $177,000 in 1925?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because of those disadvantages we suffered under the revised tariff rates of Spain. Mr. Clarke went over there and placed us in a better position, and the trade has since been increasing. The effect of these treaties and arrangements is, so far as agricultural products are concerned, that we suffer in every instance. Why is it? How does it come that these trade arrangements reflect adversely on agriculture? In this particular case the decrease in agricultural exports to Spain is practically shutting us out.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The trade returns show that in 1921 our exports of agricultural and vegetable products to China amounted to $58,895 and by the year 1925 they had increased to $4,103,000. This is a very substantial increase in tradte with a country with whom we have no trade agreement. Now let us look at the trade with some of the other places that have entered into trade treaties with Canada. For example, our exports of agricultural commodities to Italy in 1921 amounted to $56,579,751, whereas last year, after the treaty had come into effect, it dropped right down to $11,200,000. Surely the minister cannot contend that a trade treaty of that kind is in the interests of this country. Again, our exports of similar commodities to France amounted in 1921 to $12,871,679 and last year they had fallen to $4,175,000. These are the facts that we pointed out when the treaties were being put through the House, and we have striking evidence that so far as agriculture is concerned these treaties in every instance have proved disastrous to Canada. That is why we devoted so much attention to the recent trade agreement with Australia and New Zealand. Agriculture has been sacrificed by this government in the case of every treaty they have entered into with a foreign country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot quote any statistics, but I agree with the hon. gentleman as to the quality and quantity of Canadian timber available. It will interest hon. members from British Columbia and elsewhere to know that when the Wembley buildings were under construction the Canadian High Commissioner in London made very strong representations to the committe in charge, even carrying his appeal to members of the British government, to have Canadian timber used in the work. He pointed out that the exhibition had been advertised as an * inter-timperial affair and he discovered that they were starting construction with Scandinavian and other materials. I am glad to say that Mr. Larkin was successful in having a change made in the plans so that our own timber was used. I myself saw at Wembley beautiful exhibits of British Columbia timber in doors and panels. I also came across some excellent exhibits of Australian hardwoods. While I am not advertising Australian timber I am bound to say that Canadians make n, mistake if they run away with the idea that we in this country produce the best hardwood in the world. There is very good hardwood in Australia as well. They are short of the softer woods, for which they have to look to the Washington territory, but more particularly to Canada, to meet their requirements for the shipping of fruit.

Was Australian timber
used in our building at Wembley?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they had an exhibition building too. The hardwoods of Australia are not suitable for shipping fruit. It carries better apparently in our softer woods, and I think we could develop a very profitable exchange of timber with that country. They say the Australia wood is not so susceptible to the teredos as our own timber. I think some of their wood is used in British Columbia on that account.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are always training them. As I said a moment ago, representations have been made to us to appoint more trade agents. Permit me to finish the review of what the council are doing. The National Research Council is charged with the functions and duties detailed in sections 6 to 10 of the Research Council Act. I think it was Sir George Foster, the then minister, who introduced that legislation. Now, let me outline some of the work the council has been doing. For instance, take the following:
Cereal Grain Rust
It ihas been estimated tha/t Canada suffers an average annual loss of not less than $25,000,000 through cereal grain rust. No important effort was made in Canada to solve this appalling economic problem until the National Research Council, acting in close cooperation with the federal Department of Agriculture, enlisted the co-operation of the universities situated in the three prairie provinces in the organization of a co-ordinated and concentrated attack on the many problems of this disease.
An associate committee on cereal grain rust, on which each of the above bodies is represented, has been appointed by the council and (through this committee, the membership of which comprises the foremost grain rust experts an Canada, a definite programme of researches on cereal grain rust to be carried out in Canada has been established. The committee has also been charged with th rsponsulbility of putting that programme into effective operation and with the wholehearted co-operation of the Federal Department of Agriculture and the universities of the prairie provinces, has, during the past year, been actively engaged in the actual prosecution of a comprehensive and thoroughly co-ordinated programme of researches on grain rust. This work is ibeing carried on in the three prairie provinces and all facilities available in these provinces as to man power and equipment, are being utilized to the fullest possible extent.
Tuberculosis
Apart altogether from the untold suffering and misery directly attributable to the ravages of tuberculosis among humans, there is each year an appalling economic loss arising from the illness of those suffering from this disease and through the premature death of thousands of the most desirable type of citizens. In adidtion to this, it is obvious that bovine and avian tuberculosis are responsible for an enormous annual loss in the live stock and dairy industries.
Recognizing the importance of this problem, the National Research Council enlisted the co-operation of the federal Department of Agriculture in a plan for the co-ordination and stimulation of research work in Canada on this subject.
An associate committee on tuberculosis research has been appointed by the Council, representative of all the principal agencies now carrying on research work on this disease throughout Canada, and an executive committee comprised of the most eminent authorities in Canada on tuberculosis has been appointed to take charge of all work which the committee may decide it is advisable to undertake. A detailed programme of tuberculosis researches .to be carried out in Canada has: been established by the committee and arrangements: have been made for the active and effective prosecution of chat programme.
At the present time researches are being carried out by groups of workers centered at .the University of Montreal, at the University of Toronto, at the University of Alberta, and at the* research station of the federal Department of Agriculture, Hull, Que. Certain phases of the research programme are also being investigated at Queen's University, and at Queen Alexandra and Fort Qu'Appelle sanatoria.
The council have made a study of the discolouration of canned lobster. They have also conducted a research on rook crushing.

This institution if properly manned has a potential value of hundreds of millions to the country. WTe know that the success of companies like the [Kodak company and the Dupont company are due to the fact that they have scientific laboratories which have made discoveries which put them in the forefront and ahead of every other competitor. We know that the government of Canada has no equipped laboratory and no place in Ottawa, or any place else in the Dominion, to carry out this work. I am not blaming the government for that.
