I am speaking in earnest. Mr. Chairman. This Scientific and Industrial Research council, if it has efficient men and proper facilities, offers possibilities to this country that no other organization or institution in this country can possibly offer. For example, I carried a problem to them some years ago for solution. That is what this institution is for, and that is what the Mellon Institute does in the United States. If a business man has a problem in connection with his business that he cannot solve he takes it to the institute. Maybe they solve it and maybe they do not, but in many cases they do.
I submitted two or three proposals to the council myself. One was the possibility of extracting the tanning powers from tanbark which is located, as many hon. members know ten, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty miles back from the railway, where it is a commercial impossibility to bring it out; yet the properties are of great value to the country. Then

Supply-Trade and Commerce
there is the possibility of converting hides into leather. It takes about six months with the present process, and it is quite possible that it could be done in two or three weeks or a month; and just consider what a saving that would be to the country. I have made the statement in this House, and I repeat it to-night, that Canada is living off the commercial brains of the American republic to the south. Any manufacturer will tell you that. In this country we are working secondhand, so to speak. We are living off the scientific brains of the American republic, and they are far ahead of us in industrial works.
I am not blaming this government; the previous government which I supported was just as bad.
That is awful, that is terrible.
Well, I will take it back. Some hon. MEMBERS: No, no.

The government of which my hon. friend was a member passed a vote of $600,000 through this House; it was kicked out in the other chamber and never restored. No properly equipped laboratory for this class of work exists in Canada. This proposition offers the greatest .possibilities to this country. All you have to do, Mr. Chairman, is to read the evidence which we obtained in committee of this House for three years in succession. showing how institutions in the United States and other organizations had profited by the tens and1 hundreds of thousands of dollars through scientific discoveries made by institutions of this kind. For instance we know that the government of the United States buy all their material for government contracts on .the .recommendation of the Bureau of Standards at Washington. And why? Simply because they give a report on a scientific basis, after analyzing the product. That report is the .basis on which all purchases are made by the United States government.
How does this government do?

I do not know. I ask the minister to take this seriously into consideration. He has admitted that two companies have volunteered to give him $50,000 towards it. I do not say they should not. I think they should. I think other industrial corporations should do more, but the fact is that the Dominion of Canada to-day has no proper organization to devolop this scientific industrial council. In a country like Canada, with
our vast natural resources, our coal, our pulp-wood and timber, land all the other problems that are confronting this country, it is up to the government, whatever party is in power, to give an organization such as .this proper support in order that commercial organizations and1 corporations in this country may be afforded- the proper facilities to put Canada at least on a par with other countries of _ the world. This remark has reference to agriculture as well, everything is included. We know -and the Minister of Agriculture will -confirm it-that- one reason why the American republic to-day can pay higher wages than any other country is that the production per man per day in the United States is not equalled anywhere else. They have that value largely on account of the scientific 11 p.m. methods which have been developed, .and I submit that an appropriation of $150,000 for this organization in Canada is absurd. We have not facilities here for educating brilliant scientific graduates of universities, 'in order that we may take hold of the subject and develop it. Until we have these institutions this country will lag behind other countries which possess these facilities. The minister has told us about the appropriation for the study of tuberculosis, -but I do not see why that should be brought up now. This is an industrial organization. The other appropriation comes under the Department of Health, and when we come to that department I am going to say something about the dry bones in that organization. It has been sterile ever since its birth; in fact, it may be said to be stillborn. This is a scientific age, and neither the professional man nor the corporation nor the country that neglects scientific methods can keep up with competitors. This work costs money and we cannot expect individual firms to undertake it. As a matter of fact -it is impossible in many cases, just as it is impossible for individuals to discover cures in medicine. True, this has been done, as for instance in the case of Doctor Banting. But experimentation is expensive and should not be left to the enterprise of individuals or of corporations. It is the duty of the government in the interests of the country to pay more attention to scientific research. I go so far as to say that the only salvation for Canada, with her tremendous national debt and the other problems she has to cope with, is to be found in new and improved scientific methods which will enable her to compete with the rest of the world and get ahead of her competitors. If not this country will surely fall behind. I am not speaking in any partisan

Supply-Trade and Commerce
spirit to-night. In my opinion the Senate is responsible for the present condition of the organization, and I urge the minister in the interests of the country to get his government to take hold of this matter in earnest. Give our manufacturers and our business men the necessary leadership by providing proper facilities in Ottawa or anywhere else as may be deemed best, so that our problems may be scientifically investigated. I am quite serious about this 'because I have not the slightest doubt that if we do not engage in an intensive programme of scientific research we shall not be able to hold our own.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce I appreciate the remarks of the hon. gentleman, and my only fear is that the persuasive eloquence of the hon. gentleman is going to cause my colleague, the Minister of Finance, some trouble.

If I mistake not, the
council arose out of work undertaken in the first place by the Munition Resources Commission of Canada, appointed towards the close of 1915 for the purpose of inquiring into the supply and sufficiency of raw materials in Canada required for the production of munitions of war. Among the subjects which the commission investigated was that of a supply of magnesite, referred to by the minister. Prior to that time we had had, so far as was then generally known in Canada, no refractory' material suitable for use 'as open hearth furnace linings. That subject was thoroughly investigated and solved. Other matters taken UP were the supply of molybdenum, tungsten, and bauxite. These matters were brought to a successful conclusion and at the close of the war, when the commission disbanded, one of the suggestions then made had reference to the formation of such an institution as this council.
One of the difficulties in connection with a matter of this kind is, in the first place, lack of money; and in the second place, in this particular instance, we made the mistake of vetoing a proposal for the erection of a building in this city or elsewhere, which would be devoted entirely to scientific research generally and particularly to analytical work.
A million dollars could very well be spent on such a building and its equipment, and if we are to keep pace with our neighbours to the south it is absolutely necessary for us to go into this thing wholeheartedly. In the United States there are dozens, nay, scores of large corporations which spend sums of money ranging from half a million to two million dollars annually in scientific research and they incur this expenditure in the belief that they will get satisfactory returns. That belief is 
justified; they do get returns. We have in this country few corporations who have the like requisite facilities. Our manufactories are not so extensive, nor have they the capacity or capital. The result is that as manufacturers, both individually and collectively as a nation, we are falling behind the United States and other countries as well. Consider what Germany has been doing during the past quarter of a century. In chemical research she led the world and although that is not quite true to-day the fact remains that had it not been for her scientific research work Germany would not have been able to put up the fight which she did, and upon her scientific policy and achievement was founded to a large extent the German philosophy and hope of world domination.
_ We must make serious efforts along scientific lines if we hope to keep abreast of the times. The trouble I see with the present organization is the fact that, we have such a 'large number of professors engaged in the work. I do not find fault for a moment with the fact in itself that so many professors as such are on the council, but they have to devote their energies largely if not exclusively to their professional work in the colleges to which they are attached, so that they are able to give only secondary and fragmentary consideration and effort and but a very general oversight to the work of the council, meeting as they do three or four times a year, the addition of some practical men would help. What is needed is a permanent organization headed by the best man available, with several departments dealing with the various branches of trade and industry. I do not think we should bring health research within the orbit of such an institution. This should be a matter of industrial and agricultural investigation exclusively. I do not say anything against the need for investigation along the lines of health and sanitation, but that is entirely a different department, and the two branches of research should not be merged, for they have little in common. Unless this country is prepared to take a broad view and have the courage to spend money we shall make but little or no progress. We have voted $3,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway. Give us $3,000,000 for industrial scientific research and within three years results of far reaching importance will ensue.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I could not allow this opportunity to pass without saying a word or two in connection with this matter, because I want to endorse heartily everything that has been said by both my hon. friends opposite. This is something which unquestion-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
nbly must be taken up earnestly. In the department of Mines and allied branches, in seventeen small disjointed buildings in the city, research work is going on under the direction of men who are doing the best they can under the circumstances. But this is not enough. Let me say however, in defence of the research council, that they are working along lines which in my opinion will ultimately bring results if only we give them the backing they require. They are making use of the universities of Canada and are trying to correlate the work. The investigations that are in progress in Ontario and elsewhere are certainly laudable and are laying the foundations for what I hope will be something substantial in the future. I most cordially support the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite that we should select a piece of ground in Ottawa and begin the construction of buildings which will be fit to house the men engaged in scientific research. We only need to point to one investigation to show the incalculable benefit of systematic, scientific research: I refer to the discovery under the Department of Agriculture of Marquis wheat. Who can estimate what it has meant to the people of Canada to have produced this new wheat which to-day is grown so extensively in the west? That is only one thing. To-day research is going on in connection with the rust evil, and if it is successful it will result in a saving to the farmers of the west and to the people generally of at least forty or fifty million dollars annually. Once more I voice my support, in the strongest possible terms, of the suggestion to construct buildings in Ottawa to provide facilities for thorough scientific research and to make this the centre from which wiill radiate all subsidiary activity. I do think the universities entering into this field will have a beneficial effect upon the student body, and although they are costing us a larger amount of money, we will get the benefit of the investment in the ultimate advantage that will accrue to the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to endorse what has been said and go a step further. During the five sessions I sat in this parliament every session we had a discussion somewhat similar to this, but we are now just where we were then, simply because no positive step has been taken. If the minister will include in the supplementary estimates a vote necessary to do all that can be done this year to provide at least a building, which is the first requisite in connection with this work, I am confident the
House will support him. By virtue of the manner in which the money is being spent, we are not getting $150,000 worth of results. The research council is scattered all over the country, and it is impossible for its members to get together except at very infrequent intervals. My hon. friend refers to what is being done by the universities, but these are teaching institutions, and we should not mix up research work with the teaching of science, for example. I happen to know a young man who has been endeavouring to do some research work in one of our universities. He got a small grant from the research council, but it was so inadequate that he had to appeal to private individuals to pay the transportation costs on the materials he required. We ought to make a positive beginning which will ultimately grow into a research institute right here in charge of the best man we can secure for the job. It will be found that most of the men who are doing the best research work in the large institutions of the United States graduated from our own universities, but had no opportlunities to do such work here. During the war we were mining ores in northern Ontario that contained 27 per cent sulphur solely for the purpose of getting the sulphuric content. At the same time a few miles away we were transporting other ores to roasting beds, although they had just the same amount of sulphur, but we had no other means of extracting the baser metals.
I am almost converted to the view that the research council has some value. What remuneration does its members receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They got only their travelling expenses.
It is now getting late, does not the minister think we ought to adjourn?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are only a few more items to be dealt with.

Mr. Chairman, as a
representative of the agricultural industry, I can assure the minister that we will be very glad indeed to see a very substantal item in the estimates for research work so far as it affects industry.
And agriculture?

And agriculture as well. We are willing to accept our share. But I rose to call attention to the fact that this session we have had two or three very long debates and on each occasion have been told that the only thing that can save our industry is higher protection; to-night, however, our high tariff

Supply-Trade and Commerce
friends say it is research work that is needed. They tell us our industries are so far behind our American competitors that unless more money is spent in research work we must have higher protection. Then for heaven's sake let us have some research work.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Printing of parliamentary and departmental publications, including the Canada Year Book, $100,000.
Why the $10,000 increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The greater number of
publications.

I have some recollection that at one time a question arose as to mixing parliamentary publications with the Department of Trade and Commerce. What do we really do for parliament in this vote, because I think no parliamentary publications should appear in the Trade and Commerce vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, parliament is responsible for the number of copies of publications that it receives, and Trade and Commerce pays for the balance. My hon. friend will remember that by order in council in 1920 all departments of the public service are obliged to pay for all publications they receive. In 19211922 the cost was $89,000; 1922-1923, $103,000; 1923-1924, $114,000; 1924-1925, $87,000; 19251926, to February 28, $86,000.
I quite understand the printing of departmental publications, but what are you printing for parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give my friend the list.
But for parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bureau of Statistics;
sixth census of Canada, Canada Grain Act; commercial intelligence service; Canada Year Book; electricity and gas inspection; weights and measures and miscellaneous.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Trade and Commerce-Weights and measures inspection, including International Bureau of Weights and Measures, $310,000.

This simply covers the
wages incident to the employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. The estimates for
salaries of the staff is $205,475; contingencies, including rent, travelling expenses of the director, his staff at Ottawa, district inspectors

and inspectors; postage, stationery, et cetera, $104,125; International Bureau of Weights and Measures, $400. This department showed a deficit in 1920-21 of $803.73; in 1921-22 it was $14,028.53; in 1922-23 it amounted to $1,596.21; in 1923-24 the deficit was $3,265.76. In 1924-25 it showed a surplus amounting to $9,065.18, and for the year ending March 31 last the surplus amounted to $22,460.49. Apparently it is now on a profitable basis.

The fees were
increased some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Before this item
passes I would like to say a few words on behalf of the grocers and small traders who have complained many times of the charges made for examination and inspection of weights and measures. They claim that this inspection is for the benefit of the public, and that the public should pay for it. We passed a large item to-night to cover the expenses of grain inspection, because it benefits the grain growers and enables them to get more for their grain, but the grocers and small merchants are charged for the benefit of the public. The Department of Agriculture sends out inspectors, and the department pays the whole cost. One of the nuisance items in connection with the inspection of weights and measures is the fact that when your inspector goes into a store he charges $1 for the transportation or cartage of the weights. The average store on Bank street has a frontage of about twenty feet; the blocks are about 200 feet long, which means ten stores to a block. That means the cartage people will get $10 for lifting a few weights from one door to another. At every convention of the retail merchants a great many complaints are heard regarding this fee; they feel they are paying too much to have the weights carried fifteen or twenty feet in the same block. I have in my hand the record of one of the inspections conducted at a store on Rideau street. The inspection and adjustment fees amounted to $8.35. and the cartage to $1, or a total of $9.35. Every year they have to pay this amount and the merchants claim it is not for their benefit. The great majority of people receive the benefit of this work and the merchants feel that the government should pay for that inspection because it is for the protection of the people; and particularly do they complain about this $1 charge for cartage. I think the department would be well advised to look into that matter and see

Questions
why a block of ten small stores should have to pay $10 for the cartage of these few weights. I hope this will receive very serious consideration and that this charge may be done away with.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend would give the officers of the department the name of the inspector who made that charge it will be very carefully looked into, because that is not the method followed in cities.
This was done at a store on Rideau street.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The inspection of grain is a
charge on the business.

But the grain
grower gets a better price for his grain because it is inspected. In the inspection of weights, however, the benefit is to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is
wrong. He might be giving out correct weight while his neighbour might have a scale not quite correct. This inspection is for his benefit as well as for the benefit of his customers.

In the year ending March 311, 1924 there were 570,764 'inspections, of which 561.022 were verified and 9,742 rejected, which is a small percentage of incorrect measures compared to the number of inspections.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But these shops were in competition with the men who had correct scales.
It is for the benefit of the public, and we claim that the people who get the benefit should pay for it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

I think that
-winds up the business for to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Unless my hon. friends, who
have been very good would allow me to put through the civil government estimates in one block; I will not insist upon it, but there is only one increase in the whole business.

No, no.
Progress reported.
